articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Europe thinks Russia is preparing to test Nato’s limits
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: Intelligence chiefs warn that Russia’s appetite for risk is growing, as sabotage and other covert attacks target countries supporting Ukraine

Good morning. As…

blocks.text: Good morning. As the UN general assembly kicks off in New York later today, we anticipate a heavy focus on the ongoing conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and the Gulf – as well as the inevitable body language analysis of Andy Burnham’s first in-person meeting with Donald Trump.

But another related conflict is likely to dominate informal discussions: the intensifying acts of sabotage on European states that are believed to trace back to Russia but deliberately fall below the threshold for military response – a so-called hybrid or “shadow war” with the singular purpose of disrupting support for Ukraine.

As Vladimir Putin consolidates his grip on power in tightly controlled Russian elections and the Kremlin welcomed further success for the far-right AfD in German state polls yesterday, European intelligence officers have shared with the Guardian their starkest warnings yet about potential Russian attempts to test Nato resolve with an attack on European soil.

For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Shaun Walker, our special correspondent for eastern Europe, Ukraine and intelligence matters, about whether Europe is already at war. First, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: Yemen | The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.
Environment | The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months before its expected peak.

Gaza | Israeli and UK military commanders could be requested to give evidence to an inquest concerning three British aid workers killed in Gaza when aid vehicles they were travelling in were hit by an airstrike.

US | After President Trump’s snap decision to ban CNN from the White House, the four other networks that comprise the White House’s TV pool decided they would cease their pooled coverage of the president.

Slavery | Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged.

blocks.text: In depth: The line between peace and war

blocks.caption: Locals watch as firefighters work after a Russian drone attack struck a residential building in Kyiv, on 1 September. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP

blocks.text: In a series of interviews with Shaun Walker in Prague and Riga, European intelligence bosses from the Czech Republic, Latvia and Sweden raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one suggesting a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.

These sources were speaking days after Polish prime minister Donald Tusk told his parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months. French president Emmanuel Macron has also summoned party leaders for an emergency meeting to discuss similar warnings.

When I catch up with Shaun in a taxi on the way to Warsaw airport, he’s still assessing the gravity of these warnings. “One thing you always have to bear in mind when reporting on intelligence is that – because the way spy agencies gain information usually remains secret – you often don’t know if a source is talking about a very specific intercept of a plan that’s almost certainly going to happen, or if it’s less concrete chatter that analysts have put together.”

His view is that these concerns are not at the level of early 2022, when American intelligence repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade Ukraine and had hard evidence of the Kremlin’s plans (as Shaun revealed here).

What did surprise him was his sources’ willingness to be quoted: “Normally I go into these interviews assuming that we’re going to talk off the record. All of these people were happy to be on the record, which does suggest they want to get a message out.”

(Quick note, readers: “off the record” is a phrase that reporters in books, films and even real life throw about with abandon, but what does it mean? Say your source tells you about seeing a piece of fruit in a bowl. On the record means you can report that Jill Bloggs told the Guardian exclusively: “There’s a banana in the fruit bowl.” Off the record allows you to use that information to aid your investigation, but you mustn’t reveal where it came from. You can approach other fruit bowl-watchers, to check if they agree with Jill’s sighting. Then you might write: “Several sources with knowledge of the fruit bowl confirmed that a banana was present.” It’s a journalistic convention with no legal consequences, of course.)
What is this hybrid war and how can Europe fight it?

blocks.caption: Lithuanian soldiers secure the area where Italian fighter jets shot down a drone during a Nato mission, 55.9 miles northwest of the capital Vilnius on 15 Sep. Photograph: Mindaugas Kulbis/AP

blocks.text: This systematic campaign has developed since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, with common features: designed to seed chaos and anxiety among Ukraine’s allies, while it is often difficult to prove conclusively Russian involvement as Kremlin security services pivot to recruiting local foot soldiers online.

Since the beginning of this year, there has been a catalogue of unexplained fires at defence facilities supplying Ukraine in Italy, Bulgaria, Estonia and Slovakia. An explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport. Authorities in Denmark warned Russia is recruiting Danish citizens to sabotage defence firms ​with ties to Ukraine; in Lithuania, an Ikea was set on fire; and in France, five coffins inscribed with the words “French soldiers in Ukraine” were left under the Eiffel Tower. In the UK, the Rycroft review found online disinformation from hostile foreign states including Russia was warping political discourse when it published in March, while two Russian-linked arsonists who targeted property connected to former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer were jailed in June.

Given the recent escalation, it’s not surprising that Shaun observes some EU politicians “getting irritated” with the term ‘hybrid war’, and arguing that such direct attacks amount to more than “grey zone” activity.

Although European governments have become much quicker publicly to call out Russian involvement, the challenge for these politicians is deciding what effective measures they can take. After the Leipzig incident, Germany expelled more than 150 Russian diplomats and promised tighter border controls for Russians entering Germany. But the Schengen free movement zone makes this tricky: one of the suspects in the Leipzig incident reportedly entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa.

EU sanctions blacklist Russian banks and energy companies, as well as entities in the United Arab Emirates, Thailand and China for helping Moscow evade western restrictions. And there’s a growing willingness among EU nations to clamp down on Russia’s shadow fleet – ships illegally carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas.

While there are vocal critics who argue these diplomatic and economic measures don’t go far enough, others worry that even more decisive responses would riskdragging the bloc into military escalation.
“What Russia is working to is that they know even the most hawkish people in Nato countries would really like to avoid having a direct conflict.”
What is the mood in Europe?

For decades, politicians and analysts in those Baltic states most at risk of Russian aggression have warned western Europe to take that threat more seriously. But that mood has flipped of late, with the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, for example, cautioning against “panic” on social media.

These states remain the strongest voices in terms of tangible responses to Russian aggression, but are well aware that the vast majority of Russia’s military capability is tied up in Ukraine. They are also concerned about the impact that a narrative of tanks rolling into Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania has on their societies and economies – which is of course partly the point of concerted Russian psyops.
“Somebody put it to me recently – which I thought was the perfect description – that Baltic states prefer western Europe to see it as a chronic rather than an acute problem”.

With that in mind, European leaders at the UN in New York this week will be keen to create a united front and wary of interventions from Donald Trump, who has previously dismissed concerns that Russia will strike a Baltic country or other member state to test Nato resolve and repeatedly criticised the alliance.
Is Europe already at war (and what does that mean)?

When Shaun was researching his latest book, The Illegals, about Russia’s deep-cover spies, he waded through archives of KGB documents from the 70s and 80s. They often referred to “the special period”, a Soviet term that described a stage between friendly coexistence and war between communist and capitalist worlds, and was characterised by plans for relentless sabotage.
“It sounded a lot like where we are now”, he says. Like Europe, Russia doesn’t want a direct confrontation with the West but it’s clear, adds Shaun, “that their risk appetite is increasing.”

The scale of sabotage has led to prominent military voices in the UK and across Europe suggesting that the bloc is already at war – although the very definition of ‘at war’ is now liminal – and that governments ought to be more transparent with their public. Does he agree?

Shaun’s one word answer is “no”. The nuance is as follows: “There is a clear campaign from Russia, using methods that are not military, but are pretty aggressive. Some people may consider them as being something close to a war. It’s clearly absolutely nothing like the war in Ukraine.”

He suggests that European governments find themselves in a bind domestically. “If they choose to spend on defence rather than social issues, those social issues get worse and voters move to the populist right, the AfD in Germany or Le Pen in France, then you end up with leaders who are very sympathetic to Russia in power.”
after newsletter promotion
“There’s a careful path between dismissing this as a fake threat and the kind of alarmist rhetoric that we’re on the path to war and every other issue is secondary.”
What else we’ve been enjoying

blocks.caption: Alaa Hessi, an eight-month pregnant Palestinian woman, describes her daily routine in a new Guardian series detailing life under occupation in Gaza. Composite: Guardian Design

items: This week, the Guardian is following five Palestinians as they go about their lives, each telling us the story of their day. The latest moving account is from Alaa Hessi, who shares what it’s like to be pregnant in Gaza. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

I learned so many movies by heart in those turbulent adolescent (and younger) years when identities form. So I loved Hannah Marriott’s take on learning Dirty Dancing by heart as a littl’un, and why it’s her feelgood movie as a result. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

As someone who has never had the patience (or bladder control) to queue for hours for a front-row concert spot, I was fascinated by Rosalind Adams’ piece about the lengths superfans will go to, to get close to their favourite artists. Lucinda

The process of “cuckooing” – where drug gangs take over vulnerable people’s homes – is as terrifying as it sounds, but journalist Max Daly brings another layer to it in his reporting here, that shows the very complex, very human side. Jacqui Housden, newsletters team

I loved Rafael Yaghobzadeh’s picture essay about the cold war bunkers in Finland, Sweden and Norway that have been given unlikely second acts as go-kart tracks, swimming pools, children’s soft play centres and more. Lucinda

Football | The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, has agreed to commission an independent governance review after coming under mounting pressure to do so in the wake of the World Cup sale debacle.

Cricket | Harry Brook is hopeful that Brydon Carse will break back into his England white-ball teams once the fast bowler is clear of his ongoing disciplinary, describing him as a “very good mate” who is “working on a few things behind the scenes”.
The front pages

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “UK to give support to Saudi jets in bid to counter Houthi fighters”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the Telegraph says “Burnham sends RAF to help Saudis”, and the Times writes “PM agrees military aid for Saudis over Yemen”.

The i Paper has “UK fires torpedo from undersea drone in new warning to Putin” and the FT leads with “Kremlin-aided forgers moved $7bn through global banks”. The Mail leads on “New small boat farce”, the Express splashes “‘More freedom handed to new arrivals than British citizens’”. The Mirror writes “NHS need 55,00 more nurses”.
The Sun has “Letby doc: we need a retrial”, and lastly Metro says “Air traffic out of control”.
Today in Focus: The Latest

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: Rise of the far right in Germany: how worried should we be?

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office despite heavy losses in two state elections that he described as a ‘disaster’. The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland won with 38% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the leftwing Die Linke was victorious in Berlin. Merz has promised political change, but speculation is growing that his party could soon oust him. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Berlin correspondent, Deborah Cole.
Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings

blocks.caption: Illustration: Ben Jennings/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: ‘Being in an environment that’s built for you is so important’ … Amanprit Arnold speaks at an urban planning event. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: Despite 18 million people in the UK having hearing issues, there is still no dedicated centre for the Deaf community.

Now, Amanprit Arnold, an urban planner and activist, is campaigning to create one. The DeafCity Hub would be a national centre for Arnold’s community, as well as a co-working and cultural space, and a home for Deaf-sector charities. It would be designed using deaf-friendly architectural guidelines called DeafSpace principles, which include wide corridors and staircases so people can walk next to each other while talking in BSL.
This month, the project has landed a year-long “meanwhile” space (a building awaiting redevelopment), which Arnold hopes “will act as an incubator to develop this idea further.”

blocks.text: BASTE. Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte.
Facebook/ Baste Duterte
Prosecutor Lorna Kapunan says the Davao City mayor's confirmation of his local government's deals with Gencorp 'was not only an admission,' but a 'confession'

items: The prosecution said that Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte's acknowledgment of Gencorp's contracts with his city government strengthens its case in the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.
The mayor confirmed Gencorp had 19 contracts worth P33 million with the Davao City government, prompting the prosecution to request his testimony in court.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The prosecution team is unfazed by Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte‘s statement appearing to downplay his city government’s contracts with Gencorp, and said it even strengthens the need for him to take the witness stand in the impeachment trial of his older sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

The younger Duterte confirmed on Tuesday, September 22, that Gencorp has bagged 19 contracts worth P33 million with the city government since 2022, higher than the P14 million that Rappler first reported last week.
After Rappler’s exclusive report was published, the prosecution requested the impeachment court to subpoena the Davao City mayor.
“It only vindicated the request of the prosecution to subpoena Mayor Baste,” prosecution spokesman Zia Alonto Adiong said.
“He’s the one who admitted it. All the more for him to take the witness stand and put it on record for the impeachment court to appreciate,” private prosecutor Jay Tolosa added.

blocks.caption: Baste Duterte ‘confession’ on Gencorp deals could be ‘smoking gun’ – prosecution

blocks.text: The younger Duterte claimed he had no knowledge of his sister’s ties to Gencorp, and even pointed out that her name is not in the Securities and Exchange Commission filings of the firm.
Gencorp was linked to the Vice President because she declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth that she is a stockholder of the company.
Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said the Davao City mayor failed to exercise due diligence.
“He ought to know,” Kapunan said. “This was not only an admission; it was a confession.”

blocks.caption: Baste Duterte ‘confession’ on Gencorp deals could be ‘smoking gun’ – prosecution

blocks.text: “This could be tantamount to a smoking gun,” prosecution spokesman Ace Barbers added.

The impeachment court is currently hearing the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte. The prosecution has been seeking to drive home the argument that the Vice President violated the Constitution when she continued to hold business interests after she assumed the country’s second highest post. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Who is Jaime Cruz?
articles.summary: Businessman Jaime T. Cruz has figured prominently this week during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte as his name appeared either as incoporator, director, or shareholder of at…

blocks.text: Published September 22, 2026 1:28pm

Businessman Jaime T. Cruz has figured prominently this week during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte as his name appeared either as incoporator, director, or shareholder of at least six firms involving the Vice President and her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio.

Cruz is no stranger to the Duterte family. He first served as the country's special envoy for trade and investment in China in 2019 during the presidency of the Vice President's father, Rodrigo Duterte.

A Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism (PCIJ) report in April 2019 stated that Cruz served as a high-ranking official in companies identified by members of the Duterte family as having interests in. These firms are declared in their respective Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs).
According to the PCIJ report, these firms include:

items: Chinese Gen Bee Foods Corporation
City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation
Davao Bounty Times Foods Corporation
Davao Emerging Taipans Corporation
Davao New Royal Taipan Foods Corporation
Grand King Foods Corp.
Grand M.D. Business Development Corporation
Jolly General Foods Corporation, Incorporator
Metro City Chow Foods Corporation, Incorporator

blocks.text: Gerardo Del Rosario, director of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Company Registration and Monitoring Department, testified that Jaime T. Cruz's name also appeared in the company records of the following businesses of the Vice President and her husband, namely:

items: City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation
Metro City Chow Foods Corporation
Great Jolly Times Food Corporation
Davao New Royal Taipan Foods Corporation
Davao Emerging Taipan Corporation and
Davao Bounty Times Food Corporation

articles.summary: The G7 also condemns "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying that the escalation in fighting in Yemen jeopardises global energy security.

blocks.text: Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement.

The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security.

Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical shipping route for global trade.
The statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where senior Iranian officials are due to speak.

"We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

It went on: "Their reprehensible actions constitute a dangerous pattern of escalation that risks further exacerbating the conflict, undermining international trade and creating global economic instability."

"Looking forward, we will continue to support the legitimate Government of Yemen and reaffirm our strong commitment to the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Yemen," the ministers said.
Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region.
The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.
Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
A diplomatic source told AFP that France has pledged support as well, and says is ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure via a "strictly defensive approach".
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported.
Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday.
The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran.
On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified.
The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement.
Tehran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.

articles.title: Nearly 4m records of enslaved people in 20 former British colonies now searchable online
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Collection’s 300,000 pages record lives of enslaved people in countries including the Bahamas, Barbados, Jamaica, Mauritius, South Africa and Trinidad

Nearly 4m records…

blocks.text: Nearly 4m records documenting the lives of enslaved people across 20 former British colonies have been made searchable online for the first time.
The records have been digitised and indexed by the genealogy company Ancestry, which has partnered with the Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery at University College London.

The global collection offers millions of descendants across the African-Caribbean and wider African diasporas access to one of the most extensive surviving archives of British enslavement, potentially helping them uncover family histories.

The collection, known as the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers, contains about 300,000 pages recording enslaved people across former British colonial dependencies between 1813 and 1840, including the Bahamas, Barbados, the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa, Jamaica, Mauritius and Trinidad.

The registers were created by the British government after the abolition of the transatlantic slave trade in 1807, and were designed to prevent illegal trading of enslaved people and to monitor the enslaved population.

Researchers say people were recorded in the registers with chilling precision. Entries include names, ages, physical descriptions and family ties, as well as births, deaths and transfers of ownership. Some distinguish whether a person was born in Africa or in the Caribbean.

Nicka Sewell-Smith, a professional genealogist and senior story producer at Ancestry, said it was not lost on her that records originally created to count enslaved people as property were now being used by their descendants to reconstruct their family histories.

blocks.caption: An 1817 Slave Return for Nathaniel Pearce Rugless of Jamaica, former British Colonies.1 Name and position of persons making the return2 Date of return3 Fields for each return4 Names: often a single ‘slave name’. Vitally, here, most have new and old names, so a researcher might trace backward5 Col…

blocks.text: 1 Name and position of persons making the return2 Date of return3 Fields for each return4 Names: often a single ‘slave name’. Vitally, here, most have new and old names, so a researcher might trace backward5 Colour: a range of colour definitions tracked degrees of blackness6 Age: usually reputed, unless it was a child born on the estate7 African or Creole8 Remarks: in Jamaica, this entry usually identified mothers 9 Number of enslaved people

“When I use these records to unearth my enslaved ancestors, I’m using them for a purpose that was different than what it was initially intended for. Our product is restoring the humanity of a person.”
In some cases, the level of detail is extraordinary. “You can pinpoint an exact birthday for an enslaved baby,” Sewell-Smith said.

The digitisation also removes a practical barrier for those interested in delving into their family histories. Instead of needing to know how to navigate registers held at the National Archives in London, Sewell-Smith said, descendants would be able to search the collection simply by entering a name.

“There are potentially millions of people who descended from the enslaved people in the archive,” Sewell-Smith said. “Oftentimes, one of the ways that people detach from enslavement is to make an insinuation that there’s nobody living connected to these people. That’s foundationally not true.”

Prof Matthew J Smith, the director of the centre at UCL, described the registers as “the most systematic set of archival documents we have on enslavement in the British Caribbean and British colonial world”.

The release of the collection follows the publication last week of the Register of British Slave Traders, a three-year research project that revealed the enormous scale of Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. The register identified as many as 10,500 people who invested in the trafficking of enslaved Africans over nearly 250 years.

But there have been growing calls for historians to shift the focus of research from the people and institutions that owned, trafficked and administered enslaved populations towards the lives of enslaved people themselves.
“The biggest piece of the story of British slavery, and it’s also the most misunderstood piece, is the experience of the enslaved,” Smith said.

The T71 collection, which takes its name from the National Archives series in which the records are held, could change that, he said. “When you start to see the names of those individuals, and their ages, and their children, and get these very fine glimpses into their lives, it transforms how you understand the system.”
after newsletter promotion
He said the records allowed researchers to begin recovering “family stories, community stories, stories of survival, stories of resistance, stories of the search for freedom”.
Smith said researchers had been testing the data in their work on Jamaica, where they had been able to trace some families across six generations.

“It is painstaking work, but the rewards are tremendous,” he said. “It opens up a whole new way for descendants of enslaved people in the Caribbean, across the African diaspora, to understand how their heritage came to the Caribbean and survived slavery.”

blocks.caption: Pages from the former British Colonies Enslavement Registers (1813–1840). Photograph: National Archives

blocks.text: For Sewell-Smith, the archive creates possibilities extending beyond Britain and the Caribbean.
Migration and the forced movement of people under enslavement mean descendants can be found across the African diaspora, including in the US and Latin America.

“One of the things I’m very excited about is how much more interconnected it’s going to make those of us in the diaspora,” she said. “It almost makes the world smaller. It tightens us up in a way that I don’t think we even possibly considered.”
She said the scale of the collection meant its full potential would probably only become apparent as descendants and researchers began connecting its records with other archives.

“We’re in a new space, in a new place,” Smith said. “As hard as it is to look at this, it also makes me very excited for the descendants of all these people. They have a better chance to be able to get this information, to use it, and to connect with them.”
The collection is free to search and accessible to anyone who creates an Ancestry account.

articles.title: Private investigator surveilled Liberal minister and supplied Jean Nassif with recording devices, Icac hears
articles.summary: Shane de Kauwe tells corruption inquiry he was instructed by Toplace laywer Sharangan Maheswaran to investigate minister David Elliott

blocks.text: A private investigator says he was asked to surveil a Liberal minister and provided secret recording devices to a fugitive property developer, the New South Wales anti-corruption watchdog has heard.

Shane de Kauwe told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Tuesday he had installed a static camera on a building to record a person connected with the former NSW Liberal MP David Elliott.

Icac is investigating the allegation that Liberal figures Christian Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet took $2m in illegal donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif or his company Toplace in exchange for political outcomes.

Greenwood and Charles Perrottet have denied payments were for political outcomes, while Ellis has moved overseas and is not expected to give evidence. In an explosive appearance from his Beirut bedroom, Nassif insisted he was “not corrupt”.

The alleged outcomes include damage to the political career of Elliott, who had opposed Toplace developments, and the removal of the former building commissioner, David Chandler, who was scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.
On Tuesday, De Kauwe said he took instructions to surveil Elliott from Toplace laywer and executive, Sharangan Maheswaran, who he understood to be negatively disposed to the MP.
“He didn’t like him,” said De Kauwe.

He said he was asked to investigate the unsubstantiated allegation that Elliott had previously breached Covid restrictions in 2020, including the identity of a woman he was alleged to have met with, which Maheswaran wanted to give to a journalist.

He said he surveilled Elliott, at that time the veterans minister, during his attendance at an Anzac Day parade, but “didn’t find anything”. “He went to the Anzac parade, appeared to me to be doing his job, and we lost him,” said De Kauwe.
In a fiery appearance at the commission, Elliott, who is not accused of any wrongdoing, described de Kauwe as the “Maxwell Smart of the NSW private investigator industry”.

De Kauwe admitted that he used a ladder to install a static camera in 2022 on a apartment building opposite a car park with a view to capturing the woman’s car, invoicing Toplace $15,000 . Presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, asked: “You acknowledge you had no authority to install a static camera on the building where you did install it?”
“Correct, yes,” said De Kauwe.

De Kauwe detailed continued requests by Nassif to surveil Elliott, Chandler and 2GB radio host, Ray Hadley, even after the developer fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022. “He hated him [Chandler],” he said.

On Tuesday morning, De Kauwe said he had provided covert recording devices to Maheswaran, Nassif and Greenwood. He said the “two or three devices” provided to Maheswaran may have included voice recorder pens and a recording device he described as a “little square” which “looks like a a tag you would drop on your keys” and was widely available online.

He said he had given Nassif a second recording device “because he couldn’t work the first one”, saying Nassif wanted to record a conversation with two men who were allegedly asking for $5m on Chandler’s behalf to provide occupancy certificates for Toplace’s developments.

De Kauwe, who said he thought the men were attempting to defraud Nassif rather than acting on Chandler’s behalf, told the commission he reported the allegations to a contact at NSW police. The commission has heard they are unsubstantiated, and Chandler is not accused of any wrongdoing.
after newsletter promotion
De Kauwe accepted he had invoiced Maheswaran $13,400 to surveil Chandler over six days in 2021.

Icac is investigating that Strathfield Labor councillors Maheswaran and Karen Pensabene, engaged in conduct towards fellow councillor Matthew Blackmore including blackmail and possible breaches of the Surveillance Devices Act.
De Kauwe, a former Australian Federal Police officer, described Maheswaran as “one of my best friends”, saying the two became close after meeting in 2019.

He said that he was “fairly familiar” with the law governing the use of listening devices, but would often receive legal advice. Under questioning, the commission heard this included advice from Maheswaran in instances where Maheswaran was also the client.
Counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin, asked: “Do you not see that there’s a potential conflict there?”
“At the time, or even now, I trust him implicitly. I wouldn’t consider it a conflict.”
Maheswaran, who has denied any wrongdoing, is expected to continue giving evidence to the commission later week. He is currently the final scheduled witness across nine weeks of public hearings.
Pensabene has been released from her summons to appear before the commission for medical reasons. The inquiry continues.

articles.title: 4 Russia-bound Filipinos recruited for military work stopped at NAIA
articles.summary: The bureau said they were recruited for security and military work in Russia.

blocks.text: September 22, 2026 | 12:50pm
Immigration gates at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport.
Bureau of Immigration Facebook page

MANILA, Philippines — Immigration officers at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 1 intercepted four Filipinos whom the Bureau of Immigration said had been illegally recruited for security and military work in Russia.

The bureau said Tuesday, September 22, that the four were stopped in two separate incidents on September 18 and 19 after immigration officers noted inconsistencies in their statements during primary inspection.
On September 18, three male passengers identified only by the aliases "Aldo," 30; "Nery," 41; and "Baby," 38, attempted to board a flight to Thailand.
During secondary inspection, the three admitted that Russia, not Thailand, was their actual final destination, according to the bureau.
Aldo told immigration officers that he had been recruited through a Facebook post for a security job offering a monthly salary of P70,000.
Nery said he had been recruited by an unidentified individual in Bangkok, while Baby said his trip was sponsored by a contact identified only as "Alexander."

The following day, September 19, immigration officers intercepted another male passenger, identified as "King," 34, who declared Vietnam as his destination before boarding a Philippine Airlines flight.
During questioning, King admitted that he was actually bound for Russia after being recruited for military service, the immigration bureau said.
He was allegedly promised a monthly salary of P150,000, Russian citizenship after one year and additional bonuses for completing "special missions."
Immigration officers also recovered what the bureau described as a concealed Russian visa from alias King. He told officers that his recruiters had paid for all his travel expenses.
All four Filipinos were turned over to the Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking for further investigation and assistance.
Recruitment patterns
Earlier this year, Philippine authorities warned Filipinos against overseas job offers linked to foreign armed forces, following reports of Filipinos being recruited into Russian military units.
In February, the Department of Foreign Affairs warned that such employment could expose Filipinos to "grave danger and serious legal consequences," including possible loss of citizenship.

In one earlier case, Filipino Raymon Gumangan said he traveled to Russia in 2024 for what had been presented as a logistics job but was instead assigned as a shooter in a Russian military parachute regiment. He was later captured in Ukraine in September 2025.

Ukrainian military intelligence also reported that another Filipino, identified only as "John Patrick," had been killed while serving with Russian forces in Donetsk, although Philippine authorities said at the time that they were still verifying the report.

articles.title: At least two people killed in Japan as typhoon Dujuan triggers heavy rain, landslides
articles.summary:
Storm triggers landslides and travel chaos while cutting off almost ‌50,000 homes from electricity

Typhoon Dujuan has killed at least two people in Japan, while tens of thousands of houses…

blocks.text: Typhoon Dujuan has killed at least two people in Japan, while tens of thousands of houses near Tokyo remained without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday.
Dujuan – which brought violent winds of 144km/h (89mph) – was moving away from Japan on Tuesday morning, allowing authorities to downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings.

But the typhoon had already caused deaths, destruction and widespread chaos, including disruption of some events at the Asian Games and forcing the early closure in Tokyo of the one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs.

The city of Yokosuka in Kanagawa prefecture, near Tokyo, reported multiple landslides because of the torrential rain. Mud flowing into a home killed a woman in her 60s in Yokosuka, the public ​broadcaster NHK said. Another person died in Chiba.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers search a house hit by a landslide triggered by Typhoon Dujuan in Miura, Japan. Photograph: KYODO/Reuters

blocks.text: Search operations were continuing for four people missing after the landslides, NHK said.
Almost ‌50,000 households ​were still ​without electricity in Chibam near Tokyo on Tuesday morning, officials said.
The storm forced Japan Airlines to cancel 135 flights and All Nippon Airways to scrap 140.
More than 1.6 million residents in and around Tokyo were urged to evacuate on Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations were not mandatory.

blocks.caption: A boy cycles through a flooded street as Typhoon Dujuan brings heavy rain, in Ichikawa, in Chiba prefecture. Photograph: KYODO/Reuters

blocks.text: Although Dujuan weakened as it moved north-east, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area.
Oshima, an island about 120km south of central Tokyo, was drenched with 832mm of rain over 48 hours, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, NHK reported.
Rainfall in Tokyo’s Edogawa ward reached a record 282.5mm over 24 hours.

Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn. But scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water.

Typhoon Dujuan is the latest extreme weather event in a ⁠year of unusually intense rain, floods and tropical ​cyclones that have hit ‌regions across ‌the globe, from east Asia to North America ‌and Europe.

articles.title: ‘I understood what women have been going through’: fourth alleged victim testifies at Alan Jones trial
articles.summary: Executive tells court he was groped on bottom at Sydney event after ex-broadcaster pleads not guilty to 21 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

blocks.text: An executive has testified in a Sydney court that he didn’t react when he was allegedly groped by the talkback titan Alan Jones because he didn’t want to cause a scene.

The fourth alleged victim gave evidence on Tuesday in the trial of the retired broadcaster who has pleaded not guilty to 21 indecent assault and sexual touching charges. One charge was withdrawn on Monday.
The executive told the court that the only time he ever met Jones was at a event held in Sydney several years ago.
He described talking to the then ruler of Sydney’s airwaves and two other men in the corner of a room when he felt Jones’s hand touch his back, move down his spine, and rest on his bottom.
The executive said he didn’t know how long Jones’s hand had stayed there but he hadn’t reacted or said anything to the veteran broadcaster.
“I didn’t want to cause a scene … I thought that could potentially ruin the night,” he told Downing Centre local court. “To be honest, I felt a little bit powerless in that situation.”
He had not done anything to indicate he wanted to be sexually touched by Jones and hadn’t consented to it, the executive said.
He told the court he had recounted what happened to his boss that night and had confided in a colleague in the following days.
“I said I felt disgusting and powerless and it’s really the first time I have understood what women have been going through for all these years,” the executive said.
Jones had sent a thank-you email to him after the event and he had responded but they didn’t see each other again, the court was told.
Years later, the executive’s colleague sent him a link to a 2023 article about allegations against Jones in the Sydney Morning Herald.
He said the article had spurred him to reach out to its author, Kate McClymont, “because of what I’d been through”.
The executive said he had recounted the alleged groping to McClymont but didn’t authorise her to use the information.
after newsletter promotion
He was upset when he saw his allegations aired in a later article by the journalist, he told the court. McClymont is scheduled to give evidence later in the trial.
After speaking to the journalist, the executive made a statement to police, the court heard on Tuesday.
Jones was charged with one count of sexual touching without consent against the executive, which he has denied.
The executive is the fourth of five complainants to testify against Jones and has elected to face the broadcaster in person.
The former Wallabies coach has pleaded not guilty to 19 charges of indecent assault and two charges of sexual touching without consent against five men.
A charge of indecent assault against a 17-year-old boy was withdrawn and dismissed at the prosecution’s request on Monday.
Jones argues that all of the allegations – which date from 2003 to the end of his highly influential 35-year broadcasting career in 2020 – have all been concocted.

articles.title: British Columbia sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over Tumbler Ridge mass school shooting
articles.summary:
Canadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT use

British Columbia has sued OpenAI in California, saying a mass shooting…

blocks.text: British Columbia has sued OpenAI in California, saying a mass shooting at a school in the province could have been prevented if the company had warned local ⁠law enforcement that the shooter ⁠had used ChatGPT to ​plan the massacre.

The lawsuit filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence.

Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van ⁠Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police.

Altman published a letter ​to the community saying he was “deeply sorry” OpenAI had not contacted ‌law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never ‌followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says.

The school where the shooting took place is in the process of being ‌demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit.

A spokesperson for OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.”

British Columbia’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attack filed lawsuits in California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent ‌the shooting.

Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by ​suicide.

Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were first flagged by the company in June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting.
The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack.

After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the ⁠account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did ​not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law ​enforcement.

The lawsuit comes after a series of ​cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claims ChatGPT facilitated violence, ​including lawsuits related to a mass ‌shooting at Florida State ​University last year.

In June, Florida became the ​first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users.

OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.

articles.title: SEC witness: Ownership of shares evidence of business participation
articles.summary: House prosecution panel witness Gerardo del Rosario, director of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Company Registration and Monitoring Department, on Tuesday affirmed that the ownership of…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 22, 2026 12:26pm

House prosecution panel witness Gerardo del Rosario, director of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Company Registration and Monitoring Department, on Tuesday affirmed that the ownership of shares is evidence of participation in a business.
In his interjection, Senator-Judge Raffy Tulfo questioned the witness if shares of stocks are considered securities and whether ownership of shares is evidence of participation.
Del Rosario answered, "Tama po (That's correct)."
He also affirmed that ownership of a share, regardless of the percentage, is evidence of participation.
"Opo (Yes), it constitutes ownership po," Del Rosario said.
Del Rosario said a government official such as the President and the Vice President cannot participate in any business under the 1987 Constitution.

Section 13 states: "The President, Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, and their deputies or assistants shall not… during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries."
The witness previously testified that Duterte remained on the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President.

Asked by private prosecutor Erwin Matib to explain what a board does, Del Rosario described its authority over the corporation's business and property, as well as its responsibilities to shareholders and government agencies.
On the board's role in conducting the company's business, Del Rosario replied, "Hindi po siya makakapag-conduct ng business kung wala po siyang Board of Directors."
(A firm cannot conduct business without a Board of Directors.)

Del Rosario is testifying as a prosecution witness on Duterte's alleged corporate ownership and shareholdings in connection with Article 2 of the impeachment complaint against Duterte, which accuses her of accumulating unexplained wealth. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Intergenerational report underplays effect of climate crisis on Australia’s future, experts say
articles.summary: One academic says prediction for 2066 ‘is negligent in ignoring the economic damage’ on the horizon
articles.byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: An Australian government snapshot of life in 40 years has been sharply criticised for underplaying the economic and social damage expected due to the worsening climate crisis.

The government’s seventh intergenerational report, which projects out to 2066, finds the effects of global heating four decades from now are “highly uncertain”, pointing to the pace of the global energy transition as a key source of unpredictability.

The report finds sea level rise from global heating will have the greatest effects on coastal and low-lying areas, while hotter temperatures could reduce productivity of workers, affect agricultural crop yields and damage tourism. “Over the next 40 years, increasingly frequent and severe natural disasters will pose a significant economic risk,” it finds.

The deputy director of Melbourne Climate Futures at the University of Melbourne, Assoc Prof Ben Neville, said that while the report “connects demographic trends with threats on the horizon, it is negligent in ignoring the economic damage that the changing climate already is and will increasingly bring in the next 40 years”.
The report mentions treasury modelling which finds that a disorderly approach to the net zero transition result in a cumulative $2tn hit to the economy by 2050.

“As the geopolitics show, we are clearly on this disorderly pathway,” Neville said, adding that – as highlighted by the national climate risk assessment – current modelling methods significantly underestimate economic impacts “as they don’t incorporate the recognised complex impacts of climate change”.

“Not integrating this perspective when forecasting the next 40 years is a very disappointing miss, illustrating a government that just doesn’t seem to get it on climate change, all while it co-leads the world towards the next global Cop negotiations in Turkey.”

Sarah Wheeler, a professor of water economics at Flinders University said that the issue of water scarcity was overlooked in the report. “One of the largest impacts [of climate change] will be on water security issues, with higher water variability meaning increased probability of more damaging flooding and severe droughts,” she said.
“Without urgent action to address and manage these issues, the ramifications on Australian productivity and wellbeing will be huge.”

Climate activist Anjali Sharma questioned the report’s utility. “Young people won’t be looking at this report to know their future. What use is a report forecasting the next forty years by a government failing to tackle the greatest challenge of our time?”
However, the report does highlight the benefits of embracing renewable energy.

Prof Frank Jotzo, director of the Centre for Climate and Energy Policy at the Australian National University, said it “correctly points out the many economic advantages that Australia will reap from the transition to renewable energy, and from future clean energy-based export industries”.

“The national vision of renewable energy based exports of green iron, green ammonia and carbon-neutral fuels is alive, despite some disappointment of early excitement not yet having translated into large investments.”

The executive director of policy for the Investor Group on Climate Change, Francesca Muskovic, said: “The government needs a laser focus on making sure datacentres’ growing electricity demand is aligned to and supports investment and rollout of new, firmed renewable energy.

“Runaway demand without securing a strong pipeline of additional, new clean energy supply will put immediate, acute pressure on the existing grid and could lead to increased energy prices for Australian households and businesses.”

articles.title: Trump seeks ‘massive’ Belarus fertiliser deal amid Canada trade war
articles.summary:
Trump’s announcement on Russia ally comes as he steps up his trade war with Canada, a long-term US ally and top supplier of potash

President Donald Trump has said he is working on a…

blocks.text: President Donald Trump has said he is working on a “massive” deal to buy fertiliser from Belarus, pivoting away from main supplier Canada amid an escalating trade dispute, and moving instead toward an ally of Russia.

“The United States is working on a massive deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our farmers and ranchers.”
In recent weeks Trump has stepped up his trade war with Canada, a long-term US ally and the country’s biggest supplier of potash.
The announcement on Monday shows Washington’s willingness to pursue dialogue with Minsk despite its repression of dissidents and support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
The US imports most of its potash – a chemical salt used to manufacture fertiliser – and prices soared after the Ukraine war began in 2022.
In 2024, 79% came from Canada, 11% from Russia and 4% from Belarus, according to the US Geological Survey.

Washington has quietly moved to thaw relations with Belarus under Trump’s second administration. Last week, Belarus freed 25 political prisoners as the US lifted sanctions on two of the country’s companies.
But hundreds remain in prison after President Alexander Lukashenko, in power since 1994, suppressed mass protests over his reelection in 2020, which was followed by a wave of sanctions.
Western countries again squeezed Belarus with sanctions in 2022 after Minsk allowed Moscow to invade Ukraine through its territory.
Belarus’s exiled opposition leader, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, on Monday warned that any deal with Lukashenko was “very risky”.

“Our position is that it is not time to trade with the regime while all the income from potash goes to repression, goes to support of the Russian war machine,” Tsikhanouskaya told Agence France-Presse.
She stressed, however, her belief that Americans “know who Lukashenko is”.

articles.title: Hope for UK mothers accused of child abduction after fleeing domestic violence
articles.summary:
Women escaping abusive partners abroad could get new protections from legal analysis of Hague convention

British mothers who bring their children with them when returning to the UK after…

blocks.text: British mothers who bring their children with them when returning to the UK after fleeing from domestic abuse abroad – which can lead to them being accused of abduction – could be given greater legal protection and support.

The government has agreed to examine how domestic abuse features in international child abduction cases, with a view to giving survivors of domestic abuse more help fighting partners’ demands that they return children to their home countries.
The changes would come too late for Claire, who lived in the US with an abusive partner and their two small children for more than a decade. But they could help mothers like her.
“We were all terrified of him. I was in near-constant fear for my life,” she said. “Eventually, I escaped and got us all on a plane back home to the UK.”

She lived in hiding for three months, but eventually had to apply for benefits. “Within a day, the police were at our door with summons under the Hague convention to appear in court just nine days later,” she said.

Approximately 500 Hague-convention applications for the return of a child are filed each year in England and Wales. Between 10% and 20% of children affected end up being separated from their primary carer owing to a formal court-ordered return.
Claire was fortunate: she used all of her savings to instruct a barrister, and her children were able to stay in the UK.

“I barely stood any chance even with legal representation – all my evidence of the domestic abuse was ignored,” she said. “It was only because my barrister persuaded the judge to let my oldest child, who was a few weeks short of the 14 years when courts will listen to their views, give evidence that I won the case.”

The new analysis, to be carried out by the Ministry of Justice’s private international family law team, will look at all cases held in the high court in London between 2024 and 2025 under the 1980 Hague convention.
The convention requires signatory countries to return children who have been unilaterally removed abroad within six weeks so that courts in their home countries can decide on future arrangements.

Campaigners hope the analysis, the first of its kind, will disprove the four-decade-old assumptions, baked into the convention, that all child abduction is harmful and that children must be returned immediately for overseas courts to decide their futures.

Ruth Dineen, international coordinator of the Filia Hague Mothers campaign, said the convention had been introduced in 1980 to protect children from the harmful effects of their wrongful removal from their home country.

“But the circumstances surrounding international child abduction have changed substantially since then,” she said. “There are far more relationships between parents of different nationalities, so it’s much more common for families to live abroad. We also have a far greater understanding of the impact of domestic abuse and coercive control.”
Roz Osborne, head of the charity Globalarrk, said she hoped the government analysis would help level the playing field for victims of domestic abuse.

“At the moment, victims do not have access to equal legal support, due to legal aid inequalities, which causes delay or – worse – no legal representation at all for the victim survivor,” she said. “Where respondents do not meet the means and merits test and pay, they can lose substantial funds, even when winning their case, putting them in debt.
after newsletter promotion

“Victims have no access to emotional support in the high court, via a domestic abuse support worker,” she added. Summary hearings do not allow sufficient understanding of the risks victims face, often underestimating the risks. Children’s safety is inseparable from their primary carer’s safety, most often the mother, and this is not recognised.” In addition, she said, children were not acknowledged as victims in their own right, as they are under domestic abuse legislation in the UK.

Dr Adrienne Barnett, the director of Right to Equality, said there was a “dearth of basic data” around these cases. “On top of not knowing how often domestic violence is alleged and found, we don’t even know what percentage of returning parents are mothers,” she said.

“We don’t know how many cases end in children being returned without their parent, whether the children say they don’t want to be sent home or what protective measures are put in place when they are.”

Lisa Smart, a Liberal Democrat MP and long-term campaigner on the shortcomings of the Hague convention, said the analysis was long overdue. “A parent – often but not always the mother – who escapes to this country to protect themselves and their children from violence should not find themselves faced with a legal mechanism that treats them as a wrongdoer,” she said. “Yet that is precisely the situation too many find themselves in.”

A Home Office spokesperson said there was no timeline for the new research but that it was “intended to provide robust evidence to inform possible future government policy on the effective operation of the convention in England and Wales in these complex and sensitive cases”.
Alison Shalaby, the chief executive of Reunite, said it remained vital that children were returned immediately to their parents when abducted.

“The Hague convention provides a clear, unbiased court process that the left-behind parent can follow,” she said. “It provides plenty of defences and opportunities for parents under the convention in England and Wales, where legal aid is available where there is domestic abuse.”

items: In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] How the Philippines lost its salt
articles.summary: How does an archipelago endowed with more than 36,000 kilometers of pristine coastline end up purchasing from abroad seawater’s most elemental gift?

items: The author reminisces about the once-thriving salt industry in Manila Bay during the late 1960s to mid-1970s, highlighting its significance in local culture and economy.

The decline of the Philippine salt industry is attributed to urbanization, erratic weather, outdated technology, and the detrimental effects of the ASIN Law, which forced traditional salt producers to comply with industrial standards they could not meet.

Recent legislation, the Philippine Salt Industry Development Act of 2024, aims to revitalize the sector by exempting artisanal salt from mandatory iodization, acknowledging the need to protect local salt farmers and their heritage.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
I remember a very different Manila Bay.

It was sometime between the late 1960s and the mid-1970s. The exact dates have blurred with time, but the coastal landscape remains vivid through the window of our family car, with my father’s hands steady at the wheel. Back then, long before massive reclamation projects pushed the shoreline far into the ocean, as far as my young eyes could see, lay row upon row of shallow salt beds, tended from dawn to dusk under the punishing tropical sun by weathered, barefoot laborers.

Las Piñas was then a thriving capital of salt-making, carpeted with hundreds of hectares of irasan. Its prized primera salt, renowned across Luzon for being as pure and white as winter frost, graced household pantries and public markets across greater Manila.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] How the Philippines lost its salt

blocks.text: Salt feels ordinary now. Yet, for centuries, it was the very bedrock of human survival and civilization’s first currency. Before cold storage and modern refrigeration, it was what kept empires fed through lean seasons and explorers during voyages.

Governments waged conflicts and levied heavy taxes over its trade, and merchants carved historic commerce routes along its trail. Even today, our language preserves its timeless nobility whenever we honor the fundamentally decent and hardworking among us as the “salt of the earth.”
Which makes what eventually happened to the Philippine salt industry all the more bewildering and tragic.

In 1970, official records mentioned during Senate deliberations revealed that the country produced roughly 89% of its domestic salt, relying on foreign suppliers for a mere 11%. Even by the early 1990s, local beds still supplied nearly 85% of our national needs.

Today, the arithmetic has flipped completely on its head. Government estimates now place our dependence on imported salt as high as 93%. In 2024 alone, the Philippines imported nearly 660,000 metric tons valued at over $41 million — with Australia and China cornering roughly 98% of that vast volume.
How does an archipelago endowed with more than 36,000 kilometers of pristine coastline end up purchasing from abroad seawater’s most elemental gift?

blocks.caption: Cavite’s last traditional salt makers hold onto dying industry

blocks.text: The decline was not born of a single misstep. The relentless march of urbanization, coastal highways, and encroaching reclamation steadily swallowed the heritage beds of Las Piñas and neighboring provinces.
Shifting, erratic weather patterns brought unexpected rains that disrupted the delicate, sun-dependent rhythm of solar evaporation.
Meanwhile, local technology remained frozen in time, leaving our domestic producers defenseless against flood tides of heavily subsidized, cheap industrial salt from abroad.
Then, well-intentioned public policy delivered the quiet, crushing blow.
In late 1995, then-president Fidel V. Ramos signed Republic Act 8172, the Act for Salt Iodization Nationwide, widely known as the ASIN Law. Its core public-health premise was undeniably noble.
Iodine deficiency had long stunted childhood development and caused widespread goiter across rural areas, and by clinical measures, universal fortification worked.
Between 1998 and 2003, median urinary iodine levels among Filipino schoolchildren surged, drastically reducing severe deficiencies nationwide.
The benefits, however, were never truly universal, as pregnant and lactating mothers continued to suffer deficiencies that required targeted interventions anyway.
The fundamental flaw was never the ambition of public health; it was the administrative myopia of the mandate.

Instead of treating iodization as an industrial, downstream process, the state conscripted traditional, artisanal salt makers into an industrial food-fortification regime they could neither understand nor afford.

Under threat of stiff legal penalties, the law and its implementing rules demanded that every producer, local processor, and even modest wet-market vendors handle and distribute only iodized products.
Imagine what that impossible demand meant to the salt farmer of my childhood memories. His timeless trade was an organic alchemy of sun, wind, tide, and generational patience.

Overnight, the state expected him to become a sophisticated chemical processor — requiring mechanical mixing equipment, costly potassium iodate, laboratory testing, specialized packaging, and an endless paper trail of regulatory compliance.
Unable to bear the financial burden, generations of coastal families had no choice but to abandon their salt pans.
Vantage Point believes that there was always a wiser, more humane path.

The government could have easily established centralized, cooperative refining facilities to fortify food-grade salt destined for mass consumption, while leaving coastal harvesters free to produce raw sea, agricultural, and artisanal salt. Instead, a struggling, sun-baked trade was made to shoulder an impossible compliance cost.
The ultimate irony arrived nearly three decades later.
With the passage of the Philippine Salt Industry Development Act of 2024 (or Republic Act 11985), Congress finally conceded the truth.

The new measure seeks to revitalize an endangered sector by explicitly exempting artisanal and non-food salt from mandatory iodization, declaring at long last that the burden of chemical fortification should never rest on primary farmers.

blocks.caption: The solar salt production process. Courtesy of Asin Center, Pangasinan State University/Department of Science and Technology

blocks.text: Thirty years too late, the state finally grasped the obvious difference between harvesting sea salt and chemically altering it.
Whenever I gaze at the gray, reclaimed shoreline of modern Manila Bay, I think back to the boy watching from the back seat of his father’s car.
Economic growth and urban sprawl may have made the loss of those dazzling white beds somewhat inevitable, but an entire domestic heritage did not have to die with them.
We could have protected our children’s health without asking our coastal salt farmers to pay with their very existence.
I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

articles.title: BOC files complaint with DOJ vs. 14 over misdeclared agri products
articles.summary: The Bureau of Customs on Tuesday filed a complaint with the Department of Justice against 14 individuals, including nine of its own personnel, over alleged misdeclared agricultural products at the…

blocks.text: Published September 22, 2026 11:48am

The Bureau of Customs (BOC) on Tuesday filed a complaint with the Department of Justice against 14 individuals, including nine of its own personnel, over alleged misdeclared agricultural products at the Port of Subic.

According to the BOC, six complaints were filed for alleged violation of the Customs Modernization and Tariff Act (CMTA) against the owner and representatives of Berches Consumer Goods Trading and the BOC personnel in charge of examining and appraising the goods.
BOC Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said the respondents misdeclared white onions and carrots, totaling P17.5 million.
“Again, ito ay magsilbing babala kahit sa aming mga tauhan na mananagot ang mga nagkakamali sa batas,” he said.
(Again, this will serve as a warning, even to our personnel, that those who violate the law will be held accountable.)

“Ito ay utang natin sa ating mga kababayan, again mga magsasaka, mangingisda na naghihirap araw-araw upang kumita ng tama, magtrabaho nang marangal at itong mga smugglers ay hindi nahihiya sa kanilang patuloy na pagsubok na kumita sa pamamagitan ng smuggling,” he added.

(This is something we owe to our fellow Filipinos, again, the farmers and fishermen who struggle every day to earn fairly and work honorably, while these smugglers are not ashamed of their continued attempts to profit through smuggling.)
He also warned the public against the danger of consuming smuggled goods.

“Delikado kapag smuggled. Hindi natin alam dahil merong epekto sa kalusugan. Hindi sila kumukuha ng tamang permiso sa Department of Agriculture, in particular halimbawa sa DTI (Department of Trade and Industry)… Delikado,” he said.

(It is dangerous when it is smuggled. We don’t know because it has an effect on health. They do not obtain the proper permits from the Department of Agriculture, particularly, for example, from the DTI… It is dangerous.)
Nepomuceno said that the respondent BOC officials are now under preventive suspension.
Meanwhile, Nepomuceno said that the BOC will also file a complaint for violation of the Anti-Agricultural Sabotage Act of 2024 (AAES).
“Itong P17 million na ito ay lagpas sa threshold na tinatawag ng AAES. Ang threshold po ay P10 milyon. Kaya ito, sasampahan din natin ng violation ng AAES,” he said.
(This P17 million is above the threshold set by the AAES. The threshold is P10 million. So we will also file a [complaint for] violation of the AAES.)
In total, the BOC has conducted 1,882 operations, recovering smuggled goods worth P84 billion, according to the commissioner.
Of the P84 billion, he said that almost P14 billion were due to agricultural smuggling. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: SEC witness: Law does not require firms to declare dividends
articles.summary: The Corporation Code does not require companies to declare dividends it paid to its stockholders, a witness from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published September 22, 2026 11:22am
The Corporation Code does not require companies to declare dividends it paid to its stockholders, a witness from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Tuesday.
SEC Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo del Rosario made the testimony during Day 28 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

Cross-examined by defense lawyer Justin Gular, Del Rosario said Section 42 of the Corporation Code states that “the board of directors of a stock corporation may declare dividends out of the unrestricted retained earnings which shall be payable in cash, property, or in stock to all stockholders on the basis of outstanding stock held by them.”
Asked if the phrase “may declare” means such declaration is not mandatory, Del Rosario said, “Tama po.” (You are correct.)
Del Rosario earlier testified 10 of the 18 firms which the Vice President or her husband Manases Carpio have interest in did not declare dividends in multiple years covering years 2004 to 2025.
He also said that eight of the 18 firms did not submit any annual financial statements, meaning the SEC did not have information to determine if these companies paid dividends.
On Tuesday, Del Rosario testified that Section 42 of the Corporation Code provides certain exemptions in declaring dividends such as:

items: (a) when justified by definite corporate expansion projects or programs approved by the board of directors; or

(b) when the corporation is prohibited under any loan agreement with financial institutions or creditors, whether local or foreign, from declaring dividends without their consent, and such consent has not yet been secured; or
(c) when it can be clearly shown that such retention is necessary under special circumstances obtaining in the corporation, such as when there is need for special reserve for probable contingencies.

blocks.text: Gular then argued that Section 3.i of the Code of Conduct for Public Officials and Employees states that the crime of conflict of interest is only committed when a public official is a substantial shareholder or has substantial interest in the firm.
Asked by Gular if he is in the position to determine whether the Vice President is a substantial shareholder or has substantial interest in the 18 firms discussed, Del Rosario said “No.”

Gular also asked the SEC official if he has access to information on inheritance, sale of properties, appraised value of land, which could account for the assets of the Vice President other than the dividends from the 18 firms, and Del Rosario replied no since these records are outside of the SEC’s mandate. —AOL, GMA News
