articles.title: Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C. gets greenlight for expansion
articles.summary: Approval came immediately after the provincial government issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC. The project involves adding a new storage tank and equipment to produce 7,700…

image.caption: The FortisBC Tilbury LNG project in Delta, B.C., is pictured in November 2015. An expansion proposal for the project has been approved by both the provincial and federal governments. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

Approval came immediately after the provincial government issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC. The project involves adding a new storage tank and equipment to produce 7,700 tonnes of liquefied natural gas per day.
The province says the project could generate 100 permanent jobs
The federal government has approved expansion of the Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C., saying potential adverse effects are justified by the project's benefits.

Monday's approval under the "one project, one review" principle came immediately after the B.C. government issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC for the project on Tilbury Island in the Fraser River.

The province says the project could generate 6,200 full-time-equivalent years of employment during construction and 100 permanent jobs, and contribute up to $1.7 billion to provincial GDP during construction.
Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says in a statement the project shows how to "create jobs and grow the economy while protecting the environment and advancing reconciliation."
The project involves adding a large new storage tank and equipment to produce up to 7,700 tonnes of liquefied natural gas per day.

But it has faced opposition from within the B.C. government, with Kelly Greene, minister of emergency management and climate readiness, saying in July she was "disappointed" by FortisBC's decision to move forward with the project, citing safety concerns.

"For months, I have listened to safety concerns from people in my community. I raised those issues with government at every opportunity. I am disappointed with FortisBC's decision, as I know many of those I represent will be," she said at the time.

Greene said her opposition had remained unchanged since before she was elected to the legislature, while B.C. NDP Premier David Eby said his government has a "big tent," which allowed Greene to criticize the plan.
Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson called the approval "a step forward in our mission to get major nation-building projects built faster."

"Today's approval of the Tilbury Phase 2 LNG expansion project will power [B.C.] Ferries with cleaner fuel, strengthen Canada's energy security and create economic opportunities for British Columbians," he said on social media on Monday.
The B.C. government had touted the expansion as helping meet rising demand for LNG at the Port of Vancouver and improving access to fuel for vessels that travel the coast and across the Pacific.

items: B.C. government clears regulatory path for Delta's LNG pipeline expansion

blocks.text: The province said in a statement on Monday that the environmental assessment certificate included "18 legally binding conditions related to air quality, wildlife protection, greenhouse-gas reduction, health and emergency planning, and ongoing monitoring of impacts to First Nations."
It said the Environmental Assessment Office sought consensus with 12 Indigenous nations, while 13 other Indigenous groups were informed of key milestones.
The assessment process was initiated in February 2020, but the province said it was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, and FortisBC submitted a revised application in February 2026.

Transport group PISTON holds a protest along Aurora Boulevard in Quezon City on April 7, 2026.
The STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — A major transport group is set to hold a two-day nationwide transport strike on September 29 and 30 as rising fuel prices continue to squeeze drivers' earnings.

Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahan ng Tsuper at Operator Nationwide (PISTON) announced on Tuesday, September 22, that at least 70,000 jeepney drivers and operators are expected to join the strike, along with groups representing workers, the urban poor and commuters.
PISTON National President Mody Floranda said affected routes and areas in Metro Manila include:

items: Cubao-Marikina-Antipolo
Commonwealth
España
Monumento
Novaliches
Baclaran
Pasig
Taguig
Sucat
Alabang

blocks.text: Floranda appealed for understanding from commuters who may be affected by the strike, stressing that rising fuel prices also drive up the cost of basic goods and services.

"Tayo ay nananawagan sa ating mga commuters, sapagkat sa bawat pagtataas ng presyo ng petrolyo, ang kaakibat niyan ay pagtaas ng mga bilihin at halos hindi na makasabay ang maliliit na sahod at kita ng ating mamamayan," Floranda said in an interview with dzMM.
("We are appealing to our commuters because every increase in fuel prices comes with higher prices of goods, while our people's low wages and incomes can barely keep up.")
Among the groups' demands are the immediate suspension of value-added and excise taxes on fuel products, the scrapping of the Oil Deregulation Law, higher wages for workers and a fare increase.
Floranda said other transport groups are welcome to join the strike at the end of the month.
Three major fuel price hikes this September have driven up diesel prices by a total of P18.31 per liter, kerosene by P16.67 and gasoline by P15.25.
The latest round of increases took effect Tuesday, with diesel rising by P8.82 per liter, kerosene by P6.47 and gasoline by P4.88.
The Department of Energy has said upward pressure on fuel prices could persist until the end of the year as tensions in the Middle East continue to affect global oil supply.

articles.title: Bree Jonson’s death: 5 years, 2 autopsies, still no final NBI report
articles.summary: Five years after artist Bree Jonson was found dead at a La Union resort, her family continues to ask the NBI to disclose its findings

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – It has been five years since visual artist Breanna Patricia “Bree” Jonson was found dead at a resort in San Juan, La Union.
Jonson, 30, was staying at the resort with her then-boyfriend Julian Ongpin when she was found unresponsive inside their room on September 18, 2021.
The case soon drew national attention. Ongpin, the son of businessman Roberto Ongpin, was detained after police found 12.6 grams of cocaine in their room and said he tested positive for cocaine use.
What followed was a series of conflicting accounts, forensic examinations, and legal proceedings.

The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) later conducted a second autopsy and opened a separate investigation. But while the Philippine National Police (PNP) eventually said it had found no sign of foul play and no longer considered Ongpin a person of interest, the NBI’s own findings were never publicly released.
In 2026, Bree’s family renewed its call for the NBI to finally account for its investigation.

“We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for equal treatment — the same urgency, diligence,and commitment that should be afforded to every case, regardless of who is involved or how much political pressure surrounds it,” the Jonson family said in a statement on September 17, a day before the fifth anniversary of Bree’s death.

The family, the statement added, is “calling on the NBI to provide a clear and substantive status update, state whether the investigation has been completed, account for the evidence placed in its custody, and provide the long-awaited final report — or explain what investigative work remains and why it has taken five years.”
Here is a timeline of the case’s major developments:
On September 18, 2021, Jonson was found unresponsive in a room at Flotsam and Jetsam resort in San Juan, La Union, where she had been staying with Ongpin.
Ongpin told police that he found Jonson hanging inside the bathroom. He said he entered the bathroom after breaking through a small window and later brought her to the bed.
According to reports, Jonson was taken to the Ilocos Training and Regional Medical Center, where she was declared dead on arrival.

The initial police investigation listed asphyxia, or lack of oxygen, as the cause of death. Police also seized around 12.6 grams of cocaine from the room and said both Jonson and Ongpin tested positive for cocaine use.
Ongpin was arrested in connection with the drug possession case. He was initially considered a person of interest in Jonson’s death.

Then-PNP chief Guillermo Eleazar confirmed on September 21, 2021, that the La Union Prosecutor’s Office had decided to temporarily release Ongpin while the drug complaint underwent preliminary investigation.
At the time, police had yet to reach a conclusion on how Jonson died.

Jonson’s mother, Salome “Sally” Jonson, publicly questioned the possibility of suicide and appealed to the Department of Justice (DOJ) to ensure that Ongpin would remain available while the investigation continued.

The DOJ then ordered the Bureau of Immigration (BI) to place Ongpin on its lookout bulletin, allowing authorities to monitor his possible departure from the country while the case was under investigation.
Jonson’s family requested another examination of her remains, saying the initial medico-legal findings warranted further investigation.
The family’s lawyers said the initial report showed bruises on parts of Jonson’s body apart from the ligature mark on her neck, which they said could indicate a struggle.
On September 22, 2021, the NBI confirmed that it had concluded the second autopsy on Jonson’s body.
Then-NBI spokesman Ferdinand Lavin said the procedure began at about 2 am and ended at around 7 am. Specimens collected during the examination were to undergo laboratory testing.
The bureau also sent a forensic team to La Union to process the crime scene and said it would seek evidence from the PNP, which had been the first law enforcement agency at the scene.

During a press conference on September 23, 2021, police released CCTV footage showing Jonson and Ongpin outside their room shortly before Jonson was found unconscious. Eleazar said the footage appeared to show the couple having an altercation.

Jonson’s family and lawyers also said they saw a heated confrontation in the footage. They pointed to the scene as one reason they wanted authorities to take a closer look at what happened before Jonson’s death.

Ongpin later denied this interpretation. In his official statement to the police on September 24, 2021, he described the scene as a misunderstanding involving a bottle of alcohol and said arguments between him and Jonson were rare.
Jonson was buried at the Davao Memorial Park in Davao City on September 29, 2021.
Her family continued to question how police had handled the case, including Ongpin’s release and what they saw as delays in obtaining forensic findings.
The family said it was pursuing legal remedies while continuing to press authorities for a thorough investigation.

blocks.caption: Bree Jonson, remembered

blocks.text: During Jonson’s first autopsy on September 20, 2021, the PNP Region 1 Crime Laboratory removed portions of her stomach, heart and trachea to obtain tissue samples.

Three days later, during the NBI’s second autopsy, the bureau reported that the organs had not yet been formally turned over by the PNP. Jonson’s family and lawyers requested their release but said they received no definitive response over the next several days.

On September 29, 2021, the family contacted Eleazar, who said he would look into the matter. Two days later, then-PNP Crime Laboratory chief Pascual Muñoz Jr. told the family that the organs could not be turned over without a court order.
The response angered Sally, who questioned why the family had to go through a legal process when the police could have exercised their “political will” to expedite the matter.
After Sally personally raised the issue with Eleazar, the former PNP chief ordered the proper turnover and endorsement of the organs to the NBI. A court order was ultimately not required.

Eleazar later said there had been a misunderstanding. In a statement published October 3, 2021, he said the NBI had already seen the organs but could not clearly distinguish the heart, stomach and trachea tissues after they had been cut into sections and returned to the abdominal cavity.
Jonson’s family and lawyers rejected that explanation, saying there had been “no misunderstanding” about what they were asking for: the release and proper turnover of the organs to the NBI.
On October 18, 2021, the DOJ formally indicted Ongpin for possession of dangerous drugs under Republic Act No. 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002.

The charge stemmed from the cocaine recovered from the resort room. Prosecutors classified the offense as non-bailable and said the criminal information would be filed before the Regional Trial Court in San Fernando City, La Union.
The drug case was separate from the investigation into Jonson’s death.
On October 21, 2021, Ongpin filed a 16-page motion before a regional trial court in San Fernando City, La Union, seeking the suspension of the proceedings.
His camp argued that the DOJ’s resolution had procedural deficiencies and questioned whether prosecutors had established that Ongpin actually possessed the cocaine.
His lawyers also questioned how the drug evidence had been seized and handled, and argued that his right to due process had not been observed.
On November 15, 2021, the La Union Regional Trial Court Branch 27 dismissed the drug possession case against Ongpin.

According to Branch 27 Judge Romeo Agacita, police had failed to comply with several requirements governing the handling and documentation of seized drugs. Among the problems cited were the lack of immediate individual markings on some sachets and the absence of the witnesses required during the inventory.
The court ruled that the lapses undermined the chain of custody of the seized evidence and therefore found no probable cause to issue an arrest warrant.

Following the ruling, then-BI spokesperson Dana Sandoval said the BI delisted Ongpin from its hold departure order (HDO) system and confirmed that he could leave the country “unless there are other pending arrest warrants or derogatory order issued against him,” Philstar.com reported on November 18, 2021. The DOJ then said it would file a motion for reconsideration.

But according to another report on November 21, then-Justice Secretary Menardo Guevarra said the BI is still monitoring Ongpin’s whereabouts under an active immigration lookout bulletin while the DOJ prepares a motion for reconsideration and the NBI continues to investigate Jonson’s death. When asked if Ongpin was still in the Philippines, Guevarra said he did not know.
More than two months after the NBI began its parallel investigation, the bureau had yet to produce a final report.
On December 4, 2021, Guevarra said the NBI probe had stalled, according to an Inquirer.net report.

Guevarra said NBI agents were waiting for a judge to act on an application for a search warrant needed to obtain additional forensic evidence. The judge was reportedly on extended leave. Guevarra also said the bureau was waiting for the PNP to clarify information contained in its DNA report.
This was the DOJ’s last publicly reported explanation of the status of the NBI investigation in 2021.
The PNP announced on December 6, 2021 that Ongpin was no longer considered a person of interest in Jonson’s death.

The police investigation had found no sign of foul play, said General Dionardo Carlos, the newly appointed PNP chief at the time. The PNP also said it would continue cooperating with the DOJ’s investigation and respond to requests involving its DNA report.
The PNP’s announcement did not, however, amount to the release of the NBI’s findings. The two investigations had been proceeding separately.
Jonson’s case would again resurface in February 2022 after claims that then-PNP chief Dionardo Carlos had gone to Balesin Island to meet the Ongpin family and discuss Julian Ongpin’s case.

According to a Philippine News Agency report, Carlos denied the allegation, saying his trip had nothing to do with the case. Roberto Ongpin, Julian’s father, owned the company operating the Balesin resort.
Public reporting on Jonson’s case became sparse after the first months of 2022.

Beyond Roberto Ongpin’s death in February 2023, which again briefly brought attention to Jonson’s case, publicly accessible reports do not indicate that the NBI issued a final investigative report between 2023 and 2025.

In May 2026, the Jonson family’s legal team wrote to senior NBI officials asking for a review of the investigation’s status, possible reconstitution of the investigative team, and another forensic examination of CCTV evidence. They also sought an accounting of evidence placed in NBI custody.
Five years on, Bree’s family said it’s no longer asking simply for an update but for an explanation of how the case was handled.

Sally has said the family repeatedly followed up with authorities, requiring “repeated trips home from Canada,” where she is based as an overseas Filipino worker, only to be referred from one office to another without receiving the NBI’s final findings.

In a September 17, 2026 statement, the family said it is “troubled by what it sees as a disparity in the speed with which some high-profile or politically urgent matters can receive institutional attention while Bree’s case has remained unresolved for five years.”

While stressing that the family is not making a claim about any person’s influence, it is concerned by “the extraordinary length of the delay,” so it’s asking the NBI “to explain how cases are prioritized and to demonstrate that the same standards of urgency and diligence apply regardless of who is involved.”
Jonson’s family is again calling on the NBI to clearly explain what work remains pending and why the case has remained unfinished for five years.
The appeal, the Jonson family said, is “ultimately about transparency, accountability and equal access to justice.” – Rappler.com
Dominique Astucia is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

articles.title: Political fight over gun buyback after boy, 11, shot in the face and neck in Sydney apartment
articles.summary: Police don’t know if shooting accidental as Labor attacks opposition vow to scrap gun buyback announced after Bondi massacre

blocks.text: The shooting of an 11-year-old boy in Sydney’s north-west was a “tragic reminder” of the danger of guns, the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, has said while the opposition defends “backflipping” on a gun buyback.
The child was transported to Westmead Children’s hospital in a critical condition on Monday evening after suffering gunshot wounds to his face and neck at a unit in Norwest, NSW police said.
Five other people were home at the time, including four 18-year-old men and a 44-year-old woman, none of whom were injured.
One of the men was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence, while two of the other men were arrested and released pending further inquiries.
He appeared at Blacktown local court on Tuesday morning via audiovisual link, where he made no application for bail.
Speaking to ABC TV on Tuesday, Minns said it was an “incredibly distressing situation”.
“It’s the subject of a major police investigation,” the premier said.
“I understand the adults in the house are not cooperating with police. We just urge anyone that has any information about this horrible event … to come forward.”
Minns said the incident was a “very tragic reminder” of how dangerous guns were.
“Often the people who are the victims of guns are innocent people, many times they are children,” he said. “They’re very dangerous and we need less of them in our community.”
Supt Naomi Moore said on Monday night that police had no information to suggest the shooting was related to organised crime.
“It is an absolutely tragic situation, and we’ve seen tragedy across Sydney in the last couple of days; this is not far from the worst that I’ve seen,” Moore told reporters.
She said police were investigating how the gun came to be in the house, as there were no firearms registered to the property and none of the individuals had gun licenses.
There have been at least six suspected mistaken-identity shootings in Sydney since the start of last year.
after newsletter promotion
Last week, two teenage boys were charged with murder after the recent shooting death of a university student in Sydney, which police say was a case of mistaken identity.
Earlier this month, the state’s police minister denied that gang violence was out of control.

Following the Bondi beach terror attack, the state government introduced new legislation to undertake Australia’s biggest gun buyback in 30 years, with the scheme set to begin on 2 November this year.
The Liberal opposition voted with Labor in support of a buyback last year, but on Saturday pledged it would scrap Labor’s firearm ownership caps for primary producers.
The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, instead proposed a commission of inquiry into gun laws and a freeze of any buyback. Caps for farmers and professional shooters would also be scrapped.
The police minister, Yasmin Catley, called the Coalition’s plan a “stunning backflip” and said it would leave more guns in circulation.
“Our position is simple and it has not and will not change: fewer dangerous guns in circulation means a safer NSW,” Catley said.
Sloane defended the opposition’s position on Tuesday, telling ABC radio that resources should be spent on “red-flagging terrorists” and “additional policing”.
“We just think this is a government that is trying to say that they’ve made our streets safer, when this is really a very blunt instrument that’s targeting the wrong people,” she said.

articles.title: Baste Duterte: Davao City unaware of VP Sara's GenCorp interests
articles.summary: VP Sara declared GenCorp in her SALN. Her brother says Davao City never knew.

blocks.text: September 22, 2026 | 10:01am

MANILA, Philippines — Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte said city officials were unaware that Vice President Sara Duterte had declared an interest in GenCorp Industries Inc., which had secured 19 contracts with the local government worth more than P33.2 million.
Baste made the statement in a post on his Facebook account late Monday, September 21, a day before he is scheduled to appear as a witness in his sister’s impeachment trial.
“I, and all other officials and employees of the City Government of Davao, never had any knowledge of Vice President Sara Z. Duterte holding an interest in GENCORP INDUSTRIES INC.,” he said.
Baste also said the vice president’s name or the surname “Duterte” did not appear in GenCorp’s official documents submitted for the transactions with the city.
“Neither the name Sara Zimmerman Duterte nor the surname ‘Duterte’ appears in any of the official documents, such as, among others, the Articles of Incorporation,” he said.
The mayor said GenCorp underwent evaluation for each transaction and was found to have submitted the lowest calculated responsive bid or offer.
He added that all 19 transactions were processed, reported and published through the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System.
Of the 19 contracts, 13 had been completed while six were still ongoing, Baste said.
Four of the contracts were secured through competitive public bidding, while 15 were undertaken through small-value procurement.
The mayor said the transactions were above board. He also challenged anyone making allegations against the city government’s dealings with GenCorp to present verified and reliable evidence.
“I remain steadfast in my commitment to transparency, fairness and the absolute truth,” Baste said.
“This statement is issued ahead of any so-called lawful proceedings as I believe that the people, especially the people of the City of Davao, have the right to know,” he added.
SEC testimony
Baste’s statement came after the issue of Duterte’s business interests was raised during the 27th day of her impeachment trial on Monday.

Securities and Exchange Commission Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo Fernando del Rosario testified that Duterte remained a shareholder and member of the board of directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation after she assumed office as vice president in 2022.
SEC records presented during the proceedings showed Duterte remained on the company’s board from 2022 to 2025. She was also listed as a 20% shareholder.

The prosecution cited Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution, which prohibits the president, vice president, Cabinet members and their deputies or assistants from holding another office or employment during their tenure. The provision also bars them from directly or indirectly practicing another profession or participating in any business during their term.

Del Rosario, however, said it would be up to the Senate to determine whether Duterte’s continued role in the company constituted a violation of the Constitution. The SEC itself had not made such a determination.
The Metro City Chow Foods testimony is separate from GenCorp.
Duterte declared GenCorp as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

During Monday’s hearing, however, Del Rosario said Duterte’s name did not appear as an incorporator, director or stockholder in GenCorp’s corporate records. The company’s records instead identified JTC Group of Companies Philippines Inc. as its largest subscriber.

Del Rosario said a person could potentially have an indirect interest in GenCorp through JTC if that person controlled the latter company, but the corporate records presented to the impeachment court did not list Duterte directly in GenCorp.
Davao transactions
The prosecution is expected to examine the Davao City government’s transactions with GenCorp when Baste takes the witness stand.

Prosecution counsel Benjamin Tolosa Jr. earlier said Baste’s testimony would focus on whether GenCorp, which Duterte identified in her SALN as a business interest, had dealings with the Davao City government. The testimony is also expected to touch on allegations that Duterte failed to divest from business interests while serving as vice president.
Baste is scheduled to testify from September 28 to 30.

The impeachment trial will continue to discuss Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which includes allegations involving Duterte’s wealth, SALN disclosures and alleged continued business interests while in office. — with a report from Ian Laqui

articles.title: Victory Liner, bus groups warn services at risk as fuel costs soar
articles.summary: "We do not ask for charity," the groups said. "We ask for urgent action."

blocks.text: September 22, 2026 | 9:48am

MANILA, Philippines — Provincial and city bus operators warned that a fare freeze designed to protect commuters could ultimately leave them with fewer buses and longer waits after diesel prices rose another P8.82 per liter Tuesday.

In an appeal circulated by Victory Liner and signed by several bus operators' groups, the industry renewed its call for the government to lift the suspension of fare increases approved earlier this year.
The groups said fuel now accounts for roughly 45% to 60% of operating costs, while regulated fares have failed to keep pace with expenses.
"This is not a threat to stop operations," the groups said. "This is a notice that operations may soon become impossible."

The statement was signed by the Provincial Bus Operators Association of the Philippines, Nagkakaisang Samahan ng Nangangasiwa ng Panlalawigang Bus sa Pilipinas Inc., SOLUBOA and the Mega Manila Consortium.
Pump prices rose sharply for a third consecutive week on September 22, with diesel climbing P8.82 per liter, gasoline P4.88 and kerosene P6.47.
Over the past three weeks, diesel prices have increased by P18.31 per liter, gasoline by P15.25 and kerosene by P16.67.
The bus groups said higher fuel prices add to the cost of fleet modernization, loan payments, spare parts, tires, maintenance, insurance, tolls and regulatory compliance.
An impending wage increase would add further pressure, they said, arguing that higher worker pay must be supported by enough revenue to keep services running.
"No industry can survive when its regulated revenue is lower than the actual cost of delivering its service," the groups said.
Fare freeze's trade-off
The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board approved higher city and provincial bus fares in March as fuel costs surged.

The minimum fare for ordinary city buses was set to rise by P2, while air-conditioned city buses were granted a P3 increase. Provincial buses were approved for a P1 increase for the first five kilometers, with higher succeeding per-kilometer rates depending on the bus class.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. suspended the increases on March 18 before they could take effect, citing the burden on commuters already facing higher living costs.

Bus operators now argue that keeping fares below operating costs could create a different problem for commuters. If companies become insolvent or abandon routes, passengers could face fewer buses, fewer trips and longer waits.

"We cannot freely increase fares. We cannot impose a fuel surcharge. We cannot compromise safety or maintenance... We cannot simply stop operating without risking the abandonment or cancellation of our franchises," the groups said.
Fuel costs feed inflation

The appeal also comes as transportation costs have risen despite the fare hike suspension. Transport inflation accelerated to 13.5% from 11.9% in July, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.
Among the poorest 30% of households, transport prices climbed 15.3% from a year earlier.
The Department of Energy attributed the latest pump-price increases to disruptions in global oil supply amid the continuing conflict in the Middle East.

On September 15, the DOE certified that the one-month average price of Dubai crude had breached $80 a barrel, the threshold for the government to consider reducing or suspending excise taxes on petroleum products. The issue has been referred to the Development Budget Coordination Committee.
The operators said they weren't seeking subsidies or asking taxpayers to cover their losses. Instead, they want regulated fares to reflect the cost of running their services.
"We do not ask for charity," the groups said. "We ask for urgent action."

articles.title: US TV networks suspend White House pool coverage over Trump media ban
articles.summary:
White House promoted its own ‘Trump TV’ feed online after ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC decline to participate

The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of…
articles.byline: Ariana Baio in New York and Maanvi Singh

blocks.text: The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds.
The collective decision came after the barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights.

The ban was an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s battle against news outlets. After a coalition of networks including ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – which along with CNN form a press “pool” that share the responsibilities of capturing and distributing footage of the president carried by news outlets worldwide – announced they would cease coverage in solidarity with the barred outlets, the White House promoted its own feed online, branding it “Trump TV”. The channel purported to show “top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place”.
“Get real-time updates and live events streamed DIRECTLY to your phone,” the White House posted on social media. “No noise. Just the news that matters most – straight from the Trump Administration.”

It is extremely rare for a president to travel or make public appearances without the accompaniment of a representative from the White House television pool. Network cameras have provided coverage of the president since 1950.

On Monday, the ban against CNN meant that no broadcaster was covering Trump’s midday ribbon-cutting to unveil a new White House helipad. Although the White House provided a livestream, without professional boom mics and audio setup, the president’s remarks were inaudible over the sounds of a helicopter’s engine running in the background.

The president abruptly announced his ban against outlets this weekend in a Truth Social post, saying he had enough of “purposely negative stories” about him. Journalists had their press badges confiscated by Secret Service on Saturday.

“Effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President,” Bryan Boughton, Fox News’s Washington bureau chief who is also currently serving on as TV pool chair, wrote in an email to pool members Monday. The role is rotated each quarter. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” said Boughton.

In a show of support with the banned outlets, several outlets, including the Washington Post, the New York Times and the Associated Press, said they would not publish or distribute images taken as part of the White House photography pool including Trump’s departure on Marine One and his events at the United Nations in New York, until midnight ET. In a statement, the Washington Post described the action as part of a “collective effort”.

The five news networks, including CNN, wrote in a joint statement: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
Although the broadcast networks said they would withhold televised coverage, the print, radio and wire service press pool continues to provide reports detailing Trump’s movements throughout the day.

Hours after the broadcast networks’ announcement, the Washington Post said it would also withhold its photographs of presidential events from being published until after midnight ET to support banned outlets.

On Friday, Trump abruptly announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House because, he believes, they “constantly write or report FICTION and LIES”. On Saturday, reporters and other staff from the news organizations were denied access to the White House.
Other media outlets and first amendment advocacy groups responded by condemning Trump’s ban, calling it an infringement on the right to a free press.

On Monday, CNN, Politico and MS Now filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, asking a federal judge to temporarily block the enforcement of the ban and restore the reporters’ passes to the White House.

On Truth Social, Trump defended his decisions, insisting that his ban was not “instituting an assault on the Free Press”, but instead addressing “national security” threats – a claim the US president has recently used to justify building a triumphal arch and the White House ballroom.

articles.title: Embassy flags cockfighting involving Filipinos in France
articles.summary: The Philippine Embassy in Paris cites gambling, peace disturbances and littering complaints.

blocks.text: September 22, 2026 | 9:22am
In this photo taken on August 26, 2022, men watch roosters during a cockfighting match at the San Pedro Coliseum in Laguna province.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Embassy in Paris, France warned Filipinos against holding illegal cockfights after French authorities flagged gambling and cockfighting activities involving members of the Filipino community.
The embassy said it had also received reports of disturbances to the peace and littering linked to the activities.
It reminded Filipinos that illegal cockfighting is considered animal cruelty in France and may carry hefty penalties.

"Filipinos in France are therefore advised that illegal cockfighting is an act of animal cruelty punishable in France by three-year imprisonment and a fine of 45,000 euros," the embassy said in an advisory.
The embassy also urged Filipinos living and working in France to observe local laws.
"Let us maintain the good name and reputation of the Filipino community with our French hosts," it said.

Cockfighting, or "sabong," is legal in the Philippines under certain regulations. Presidential Decree 449, or the Cockfighting Law of 1974, limits authorized cockfights to licensed cockpits and specified occasions, while unauthorized cockfighting is prohibited. Online or "e-sabong" operations are also banned under Executive Order No. 9 issued in 2022.

articles.title: Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
articles.summary: Sinkevičius told BBC Newsnight Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Moscow, but the nation was prepared to "fight back" if attacked.

blocks.text: Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.

He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.
Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.
"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC.
"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."
Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".
It comes just a week after Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.

Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.
The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.
"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."
Moscow did not comment on the incident.

articles.title: PISTON to hold 2-day transport strike vs oil price hike on Sept. 29-30

Transport group PISTON announced on Tuesday that it would hold a two-day transport strike next week to protest against the continued rise in fuel prices.

PISTON president Mody Floranda said the strike will be held nationwide on Tuesday, September 29, and Wednesday, September 30, to be participated in not just by drivers and operators but also labor and urban poor groups, according to a report by Allan Gatus on Dobol B TV.
The strike will be conducted to call on the government to act swiftly against the big-time oil price hike in the country.
Floranda said they will continue protesting until the government removes the excise tax and value added tax on fuel products, to bring down its prices.
He made the announcement as the group held a protest action on Aurora Boulevard corner Westpoint Street in Cubao, Quezon City on Tuesday morning.
PISTON held Tuesday's protest action as fuel companies raised pump prices anew, with the increase in diesel price at around P7.80 per liter, amid the Middle East conflict.
The group ended the protest action peacefully past 8 a.m.

Members of the Quezon City Police District, Traffic and Transport Management Division of the Quezon City local government unit, and Metropolitan Manila Development Authority were in the area to maintain peace and order. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Wanted: UN secretary-general as ‘mediator-in-chief’
articles.summary: The race for the world’s foremost diplomat shines a spotlight on the crises the global organization faces

blocks.text: I had given little thought to the ongoing contest for a new United Nations secretary-general until I read the captivating book, Peacemaker: U Thant, the United Nations and the Untold Story of the 1960s. It schooled me in the dynamics of UN leadership and the ways powerful countries steered the global organization’s direction.
Soon, the UN General Assembly will choose the successor to the current secretary-general, Antonio Guterres, whose term ends in December this year.

More than ever, I appreciate the thankless work of the secretary-general, having gained a close-up view of ten years of Thant’s legendary leadership of the UN. He was the first non-white, the first Asian to hold the post.

The first two secretaries-general were from Norway and Sweden. When Thant stepped down in 1971, he was succeeded by one more from Europe (Austria). The only other Asian was Ban Ki-moon from South Korea (2007-2016). Only one secretary-general has come from the Middle East (Egypt); the same is true for Latin America (Peru) and Africa (Ghana). Guterres is from Portugal, the fourth from Europe.

Thant led the UN at a time of turbulent conflicts, from the Cuban missile crisis to the six-day Arab-Israel war to the Vietnam war. What is little known is that Thant’s mediation between the US and USSR helped prevent a third world war over Cuba. He also consistently advocated for détente during the Cold War.

Thant tirelessly worked to attain peace in various flashpoints in the world, finding diplomatic solutions to what seemed to be impossible situations, like helping broker a ceasefire between India and Pakistan in 1965.
Newly independent countries joined the UN as a wave of decolonization swept the early 1960s. Thant provided moral leadership at this critical period of transformation, championing racial equality.
It’s the “loneliest job in the world,” Thant said of the UN secretary-general’s work. But he got along with almost everyone and was respected by many.

The book opens with a farewell lunch for Thant in December 1971 where the guests ranged from John Lennon to Jacques Costeau. It was there that Lennon first sang a song he had recently written about peace, which, he said, he had never performed before in America. That song was “Imagine.”

The book is beautifully written by Thant Myint-U, a historian, former UN official, and Thant’s grandson. Unearthing rich archives, including private papers in the care of his mother (Thant’s daughter) and her personal memories, Thant Myint-U gives a ringside view of how Thant made decisions, consulting colleagues he trusted, and their verbal exchanges. His relations with leaders of the US and USSR are well documented in the book, including their conversations and letters.
Today, eight candidates are in the race for the 10th UN secretary-general, five are women and three are men. If a woman is selected, she will be the first female to lead the UN.
Six of the aspirants are from Latin America while two are from Africa.

The next secretary-general will be appointed by the 193-member General Assembly on the Security Council’s recommendation. The five permanent members — France, Britain, China, Russia, and the United States — have a veto on the final decision.
In August, when the Security Council held a second informal vote, Guyana’s ex-foreign minister, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, narrowly led this round, according to a news report.
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, head of the UN Trade and Development, was the front-runner when the Security Council did a first informal vote behind closed doors and by secret ballot.

The next secretary-general will take over at a very difficult time, with the UN presence not seen or felt in the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, and the civil war in Sudan. After all, isn’t it the UN’s core mission to keep peace?

On other fronts, multilateralism is under attack from the US, the Security Council is deadlocked, and the UN faces an “imminent financial collapse” because the US and other countries have not paid their dues
The crisis facing the UN is “very acute,” Thant Myint-U said in an interview with The Financial Times. Asked what kind of leader the UN needs now, he replied:

“…someone who is going to be good as the mediator-in-chief. That requires diplomatic skill, experience… an even temperament… degree of equanimity, a willingness to take risks and fail and move on, someone who’s willing not to always take the credit but sometimes to take the blame unfairly… More importantly, someone who has political courage, someone who’s going to take those initial risks in the interest of peace.”
I’m waiting with bated breath to see who the next secretary-general will be and, fingers crossed, she/he opens a new chapter for the UN.
Let me know what you think. You can email me at marites.vitug@rappler.com.
I will be taking a year-long book leave next month although I may write occasional pieces. My regular newsletters will resume when I return in October 2027.
Till next year!

articles.title: NATO will share Arctic responsibility as Greenland security deal with U.S. moves forward, Denmark says
articles.summary: Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. are to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to…

image.caption: Sermitsiaq mountain is seen beyond houses in Nuuk, Greenland. Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. are to sign a deal on Greenland's security at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. (Tim Barsoe/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. are to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington ‌and Copenhagen.
Denmark and Greenland say deal will benefit Arctic island and respect its sovereignty

The agreement, to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York at 10:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, has not been made public. Denmark and Greenland say the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty.
The deal is expected to allow the U.S., which already has one military base in Greenland, to expand its military presence to two additional sites.

One of those sites is Narsarsuaq, whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since ​the U.S. closed its Cold War-era Bluie West One military base there in the 1950s. The other ​is Mestersvig, a military outpost currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a special forces unit that enforces Danish sovereignty in the territory, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Trilateral signing ceremony planned

U.S. President Donald Trump will meet in New York on Tuesday with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik ​Nielsen for a trilateral signing ceremony, a White House official said.

The deal follows months of pressure from Trump, who has said the U.S. should ⁠control Greenland and at times refused to ⁠rule out using military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory. His threats peaked ‌in January, triggering a diplomatic crisis within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the military defence alliance, and pushing Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

The agreement "will be in a form where responsibility for security in the Arctic is not only Danish or American," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sunday. He said that, to a large extent, "it would be NATO that looks after the Arctic."
It remained unclear whether the deal ⁠amends an existing 1951 defence agreement that is the legal basis for the U.S. presence in Greenland.
"It appears that we are now using this crisis to try to strengthen NATO's cohesion through Greenland," said Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS).
Strategic interest in Greenland

Washington's strategic interest in Greenland dates back to the Second World War. In 1941, the U.S. signed a deal with Danish envoy ‌Henrik Kauffmann, who acted without authority from his country, then under German occupation.
Does Iceland feel threatened by Trump's expansionist threats? | Hanomansing Tonight

The U.S. sought the deal to keep Greenland out of German hands and secure the North Atlantic supply route between North America and Europe. Under the agreement, the U.S. built airfields, naval facilities and weather stations across the island, reaching around 5,500 military personnel by 1943, according to DIIS.

In 1946, then-U.S. president Harry Truman sought to buy the island as a strategic asset for $100 million US in gold, but Copenhagen declined ​to sell. Instead, a new agreement was signed in 1951 that gave the U.S. military extensive rights in Greenland but was tied to the existence of NATO.
"I don't think Denmark and Greenland will sign if the same NATO clause isn't included," ⁠said Gad.
Cold War presence
During the Cold War, the U.S. maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 ⁠U.S. military personnel.
A NATO spokesperson said on Saturday that the alliance welcomed the new agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and co-operation in this vital region."
Rasmussen, who travelled to ⁠New York ⁠overnight, declined to discuss the contents of the agreement.
"But we have ​said from the start that we are open to accommodating the United States' legitimate security interests," he told Danish news agency Ritzau on Monday.

items: Trump says deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in Greenland
Greenland, Denmark say deal with U.S. will not cede sovereignty

blocks.text: Trump said in a social media post on Friday the agreement gave the U.S. "permanent control over ⁠security, and all other needs, in Greenland," and that no U.S. adversary could have a base or military presence there without Washington's written approval.

Denmark has not responded to Trump's assertion, though Copenhagen earlier acknowledged it underinvested in Greenland's defence for decades and has pledged to expand its military presence on the island, including more NATO troops.
Greenland's government has sought to reassure the public about the deal.

Erik Jensen, an opposition lawmaker in Greenland, wrote on social media that he had read the draft agreement. "I feel reassured and am not worried," he said, adding that the island's foreign minister was handling the work ⁠well.

articles.title: Trump and Mamdani appear friendly after ‘wide-ranging’ meeting at Gracie Mansion
articles.summary:
Republican president said he hoped the democratic socialist would be a ‘great mayor’ for New York City

Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for…
articles.byline: José Olivares in New York and David Smith in Washington

blocks.text: Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms.

At a news conference following their closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion, Trump and Mamdani appeared friendly as they have in previous meetings. Mamdani said he and Trump held a “wide-ranging” discussion, which touched on affordable housing and immigration, but did not offer extensive details regarding any disagreements between them.

Asked whether he challenged Trump over his decision to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from White House grounds, Mamdani said: “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in.”

“It’s interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Trump chimed in, pointing to the large assembly of press on the lawn.

The visit to Gracie Mansion, ahead of the president’s speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday, was a measure of Trump’s apparent respect for the 34-year-old mayor of his native New York. It was the first presidential visit to the historic riverside residence in 45 years, following Ronald Reagan, who met there with Ed Koch in 1981.

Pressed on why he had invited Trump, Mamdani said he was willing to work with anybody who could “deliver” for New Yorkers, and highlighted their shared interest in building thousands of new housing units at Sunnyside Yard in Queens. For his part, Trump said he believed Mamdani had “great potential”.

It was the latest unlikely meeting between Trump, a rightwing populist who has targeted immigrants and Muslims, and Mamdani, a democratic socialist who was born in Uganda and is New York’s first Muslim mayor.
Trump has focused his midterm election campaign on denouncing Democrats as “godless communists” who seek to abolish borders and prisons and pose the greatest threat that the US has ever faced.

Yet on Monday he said of Mamdani, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America: “I certainly hope he will be a great mayor. You have to understand – I want what’s good for New York. I want what’s good for the country ... I want him to be a great mayor.”
The body language again seemed amicable. Trump deferentially stood aside as Mamdani spoke from the lectern and, when the press conference finished, gave him an affectionate double tap on the arm.
Trump, Mamdani, Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles and Mamdani’s chief of staff Elle Bisgaard-Church were all in attendance during Monday’s meeting.
Mamdani said that they discussed the Trump administration’s stripping of protections for Haitian immigrants.

“I shared my very strong opinions about how we can keep New Yorkers safe, how we can keep immigrant New Yorker safe, and how important immigrant New Yorkers, especially Haitian New Yorkers, are – not only to the fabric of our city, but also to our city’s economy,” Mamdani said.
“The president and I have been very frank about the many disagreements we have,” he added.

The meeting came one day after Mamdani, and Clara Brugada, the mayor of Mexico City, met with migrant delivery workers in New York City, who expressed precarity and fear surrounding the increase in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests.

Earlier this month, Mamdani helped initiate a lawsuit against the Trump administration for its “public charge” rule change targeting immigrant communities. The lawsuit was filed by the State of New York and 21 other states against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and various of its agencies. It is unclear if they discussed the lawsuit during the meeting.

articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Baste Duterte says he's unaware of VP Sara's alleged link to GenCorp
articles.summary: Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte said he and other city government officials and employees were not aware of Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged link to GenCorp Industries Inc.

blocks.text: Published September 22, 2026 8:45am
Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte said he and other city government officials and employees were not aware of Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged link to GenCorp Industries Inc.
In a statement late Monday evening, Baste said the Davao City government's transactions with GenCorp reached over P33.2 million across 19 contracts.
“I, and all other officials and employees of the City Government of Davao, never had any knowledge of Vice President Sara Z. Duterte holding an interest in GENCORP INDUSTRIES INC.,” he said.

“Furthermore, neither the name Sara Zimmerman Duterte nor the surname "Duterte" appears in any of the official documents, such as, among others, the Articles of Incorporation, submitted by GENCORP INDUSTRIES INC. across the 19 contracts and transactions in question,” he added.
Baste is scheduled to testify in her sister’s impeachment trial from September 28 to 30.
He pointed out that GenCorp was evaluated in each transaction and determined to have submitted the lowest calculated responsive bid or offer.
The Davao City mayor also said all 19 transactions had been processed, reported, and published on the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS).
According to him, the transactions were above board.
Of the 19 contracts with GenCorp, Baste said 13 had been completed while six remained ongoing.
Four contracts were secured through competitive public bidding, while the other 15 were undertaken through small-value procurement, he added.

“I remain steadfast in my commitment to transparency, fairness and the absolute truth. This statement is issued ahead of any so-called lawful proceedings as I believe that the people, especially the people of the City of Davao, have the right to know,” Baste said.
The Vice President declared GenCorp as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN)
However, GenCorp did not list her as an incorporator or director based on the firm’s General Information Sheet and Audited Financial Statement submitted to the SEC.
This was confirmed by SEC Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo Fernando del Rosario on Monday, Day 27 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Another Marineland beluga has died after being moved to Chicago aquarium
articles.summary: A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health since arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday.

image.caption: Belugas swim in a tank at Marineland June 29. Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says another whale from the Ontario park has died after being transported there in July. (Carlos Osorio/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New
A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health since arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday.
Whale was 4th to die after being moved from the Niagara Falls, Ont., park in July
The park said 26-year-old Osiris died Monday morning. The female beluga was one of 10 that came to Shedd from Marineland, the shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont.
It was part of the world's biggest collective move of captive whales. Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its animals.

Over a series of moves beginning in July, Marineland moved 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums abroad: Shedd in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio, Texas, and San Diego, Calif., Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.
Osiris was "not a consistent eater" but had improved recently after receiving fluids and medication, Shedd said.
"Our care team observed sudden changes this morning in both Osiris's behaviour and respiratory patterns," Shedd said in a statement.

items: Belugas transferred from Niagara Falls are under round-the-clock monitoring after deaths: Chicago aquarium
Marineland beluga from Niagara Falls, Ont., dies at Spain aquarium, 3rd death after rescue transfer

blocks.text: "Respiratory rates are one of many measures we track closely and continuously, as changes can signal that an animal may need additional support. The team moved Osiris to the medical habitat, so immediate care could be provided if needed. Her condition declined rapidly, and Osiris passed away despite lifesaving efforts by our veterinary and animal care teams."
The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.
Final Marineland whales moved to the U.S.
Two other Marineland whales, Rain and Peekachu, died at Shedd within weeks of the move. One longtime Shedd resident beluga, Beethoven, also recently died.
All are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.
Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic in Spain last week.
The whales were cleared by veterinarians at Marineland and the other parks to move and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also signed off on the relocation.
Last week, Shedd said it is concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord.

"Secord has not yet been consistently taking in the amount of food teams would like to see, even as they try different feeding approaches and offer different types of herring to gauge her preference," Shedd said in a blog post last week.

Marineland originally sought to move the whales to China after securing a deal to sell all 30 of its belugas to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, which has a Guinness Book of World Record for the largest aquarium in the world.

items: Another beluga whale sent from Marineland to Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has died
Canada's last captive whales are set to leave Niagara Falls, Ont., Marineland for U.S. aquariums
Animal Justice urges investigation into Marineland beluga death in Chicago, wants relocation efforts halted

blocks.text: Thompson blocked that move, saying it was not in the best interest of the whales and inconsistent with a 2019 federal law. That law banned whale and dolphin captivity and performances, but grandfathered in Marineland's whales. It also banned breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its whales by sex.
Marineland turned to an American-led consortium to house the world's biggest pod of captive belugas, but they needed five aquariums to house them all.
There are no breeding or performing restrictions at the belugas' new homes.
Marineland's whales had struggled in recent years. Nineteen belugas and one killer whale died at the park between 2019 and 2025.
The park blames some of those deaths on the new federal laws.

articles.title: Trump approval falls to record low as high costs bite, poll finds
articles.summary: Democrats currently lead Republicans by 8 points in voter preference for the midterms, and Trump's approval ratings on immigration and crime are also low, raising concerns about the Republican…

blocks.text: TRUMP. US President Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One at Morristown Municipal Airport in Morristown, New Jersey, US, July 31, 2026
Daniel Heuer/Reuters

Democrats currently lead Republicans by 8 points in voter preference for the midterms, and Trump's approval ratings on immigration and crime are also low, raising concerns about the Republican party's prospects

items: US President Donald Trump's approval rating has dropped to 32%, the lowest of his career, largely due to dissatisfaction among Republicans regarding his handling of inflation and the ongoing Iran war.
The poll indicates that only 17% of respondents approve of Trump's management of the cost of living, which is a key issue for voters ahead of the November midterm elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump’s approval rating fell to 32% – the lowest of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The poll, completed on Sunday, September 20, was conducted over a four-day period that saw Trump throw three major news organizations out of the White House and Washington’s iconic Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts – named after slain President John F. Kennedy – could be torn down if Trump’s own name could not be added to it.
It found voters leaning away from supporting Trump’s fellow Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
Trump’s overall approval was down from a reading of 35% in last week’s Reuters/Ipsos poll, with support among his own Republicans down to 73% from 82% a week earlier.

Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was sworn in, he enjoyed a 47% approval rating.
Just 17% of respondents in the new poll approved of his handling of the cost of living – the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November.
Dissatisfaction among Republicans on inflation has been growing since Trump launched the war on Iran in February that has pushed gasoline and diesel prices sharply higher.
Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up – 51% to 44%.

Trump’s approval rating is lower than any recorded for his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, whose presidency was also marked by surging inflation and who ultimately ended his reelection bid after a poor debate performance heightened concerns about his age. Biden’s low was 35%, reached in late October 2024.

Only 34% of the most recent poll respondents approve of the strikes on Iran. The conflict has cut the world off from a significant slice of the oil and gas produced in the Middle East, and threatens to stoke higher inflation in the US and elsewhere as businesses pass on higher fuel costs to consumers.
Trump initially said the conflict would last a few weeks and that Iran needed to be bombed to stop it from developing nuclear weapons.

Earlier this month, the Republican leader pledged the war would end “immediately after” the election. But Iran has shown no sign of giving up and in recent weeks Tehran and its allies have threatened further disruptions to oil markets.
Some 82% of poll respondents – including nine in 10 Democrats and three-quarters of Republicans – said the conflict would likely go on for an “extended period of time.”

The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed registered voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans – 43% to 35% – when asked how they would vote in the midterms. The 8-point gap was the biggest lead for Democrats in Reuters/Ipsos polling this year.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his term.

The poll results on congressional voting plans provide an overall view of which party Americans nationwide want to see ​in charge in Congress, though the results don’t capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the ​Senate and House of Representatives.
Trump remains popular among Republicans on the issue of immigration – with 79% of his party backing him – but only 36% of Americans overall support his approach to the matter and 55% disapprove.

Some Republican allies in Congress have warned that his aggressive campaign to deport people in the country illegally risks alienating voters with families who recently immigrated to America, like some Hispanics.
Some 35% of poll respondents approve of Trump’s approach to fighting crime, compared to 50% who disapprove.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered 1,277 responses from US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of 3 percentage points. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Flights resume across US north-east after FAA communications failure
articles.summary: Thousands of flights were delayed or canceled after a primary line failed and a backup fiber-optic cable was severed Airport operations across the US north-east resumed Monday evening after a…

blocks.text: Airport operations across the US north-east resumed Monday evening after a communications line failure snarled flights at some of the country’s busiest airports, leading to thousands of flight cancellations and delays.

Flights were halted at several airports after a primary communications line failed at a key Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility in Philadelphia. The backup fiber optic line, which delivers internet service, was inadvertently severed by a railroad construction crew, resulting in a telecommunications crash and hundreds of canceled flights at Newark, LaGuardia, JFK, Philadelphia and Boston airports.
Transportation secretary Sean Duffy said in a Monday evening social media post that the backup lines had been fixed and all affected airports were again operating.
“It will take some time to clear all existing delays, so please check with your airline for the latest information,” Duffy wrote.
The technical problems stem from the same FAA facility in Philadelphia that caused numerous disruptions at Newark Liberty international airport in the spring of 2025.

Regional control centers like these have two lines that carry radar and communications data in and out: the primary and the backup. The FAA said a circuit on the primary failed Monday morning, and when the system tried to switch to the backup, workers discovered that the fiber optic line had been cut.

Earlier in the day, Duffy said an Amtrak construction crew was to blame. Amtrak, however, pointed to a New Jersey Transit construction crew that was working in the area between Newark and New Brunswick, New Jersey.

The disruption coincided with the publication of a government accountability office (GAO) report, which found that the FAA has yet to finish risk assessments or update security documentation covering threats from spoofing, jamming and other attacks on the radio spectrum – prompting a prominent senator to warn of a “major threat” to national security.
The FAA also lacks a real-time system to detect all such threats, the report said, meaning it can generally only investigate incidents after they are reported.

Investigators warned that a hacker could send fraudulent messages, such as false cancellations of flight clearances, to aircraft, with the potential to cause delays, disrupt airspace or create safety risks. Two systems used to send text messages to aircraft predate modern cybersecurity standards and lack common protections such as encryption, according to the report.

The watchdog’s findings prompted calls for swift action. “The FAA’s failure to require the aviation industry to use secure communications is a major threat to US national security, to our economy and the safety of the flying public,” said Ron Wyden, the US senator for Oregon, who has long campaigned on privacy, surveillance and cybersecurity issues.
“The FAA needs to issue new standards, as soon as possible, to protect the security of airline communications.”

The GAO made nine recommendations, including a formal risk assessment of seven of eight reviewed systems, continuous monitoring for interference, spoofing and jamming, and formal guidance on information sharing. The Department of Transportation, replying for the FAA, agreed with all nine.

Monday’s disruption is the latest in a run of problems around Newark. In April 2025, an outage blanked controllers’ screens for roughly 60 to 90 seconds and cut their contact with aircraft, prompting the FAA to halt departures. The FAA later moved the Philadelphia Tracon to a new fiber-optic link with New York on two separate paths, as part of measures to improve reliability.
The FAA handles more than 44,000 flights a day and about 3 million passengers, the GAO noted.

Wyden, who sits on the Senate intelligence committee, added: “This sobering report from [the] GAO reveals that the technology used by air traffic controllers to communicate with aircraft is incredibly insecure, can be intercepted, impersonated, and jammed, and that hackers and foreign governments can exploit these vulnerabilities to disrupt air travel and even put passengers at risk.”
The GAO also pointed to jamming and spoofing abroad. Estonia and Finland have accused Russia of interfering with satellite navigation in their airspace, which Moscow denies.
One incident last September involved a Spanish military jet carrying the country’s defense minister.
The Associated Press contributed

articles.title: US judge declines to block transfer of wildlife refuge land to Musk’s SpaceX
articles.summary: Environmental groups vow to continue opposition to deal that would expand site for Elon Musk rocket company A federal judge on Monday refused to block the Trump administration from giving SpaceX more…

blocks.text: A federal judge on Monday refused to block the Trump administration from giving SpaceX more than 700 acres of wildlife refuge as part of a land swap in Texas, while environmental groups vowed to continue their legal challenge.

US district judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr declined the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction to prevent the parcel exchange, saying they failed to prove it would worsen ecological risks to a Gulf coast region already transformed by billionaire Elon Musk’s rocket operations.

In June, the US Fish and Wildlife Service approved moving forward with the deal with SpaceX, which would surrender 683 acres the company owns in exchange for the federal land in the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge. The 103,000-acre refuge spans four counties along the Texas border and is home to animal habitats and historical landmarks.
Maps show the land SpaceX would acquire would be closer to the company’s launchpad near the US-Mexico border.

The swap amounts to a gift of public lands to SpaceX, “clearing the way for bulldozers to tear into this wildlife refuge as soon as next week and turn a public treasure into a private payday”, said Laiken Jordahl, a spokesperson with the Center for Biological Diversity, which filed the lawsuit alongside other opponents including tribal groups. Jordahl said Monday that the litigation will continue even as the exchange goes forward.

“This court order is not the final word. These lands hold incredible spiritual, historical and conservation value for the people and wildlife of South Texas. We won’t stop fighting to keep this irreplaceable public wildlife refuge safe from SpaceX bulldozers,” Jordahl said in a statement.

The lawsuit asks the federal court to halt the exchange, which has worried SpaceX opponents in the area who have long criticized the company’s expanding footprint over lost access to beaches and concerns over exploding rockets.
The Fish and Wildlife Service did not respond to a request for comment on Monday’s decision. Previously, a spokesperson had said the agency does not comment on ongoing litigation.

The agency issued a final environmental assessment report in June that determined the exchange would cause no significant impact to the area. The report said the federal government believed the acquisition would represent a “net conservation benefit” and provide “substantial long-term conservation value and improving landscape-scale habitat connectivity across refuges in south Texas”.
The judge said that the plaintiffs offered “relatively weak” evidence of environmental harm.

“While they rightfully argue that the preservation of wildlife and historical lands furthers the public interest, they present no evidence demonstrating that the Property will suffer aesthetic, environmental, cultural, or historical degradation during the pendency of this lawsuit,” Rodriguez wrote in his ruling.

In addition, the judge said a preliminary injunction would result in modifications to SpaceX’s development plans, “placing additional hardship on the company’s ability to meet milestones and contractual obligations”.
SpaceX did not return an email seeking comment on the judge’s ruling.

The space exploration company first broke ground in Texas more than a decade ago and has expanded rapidly, so much that SpaceX employees last year voted to incorporate their own local government called Starbase.
