articles.title: Global diesel prices hit record highs, further rises possible
articles.summary: Refineries worldwide are operating at maximum capacity, with the US experiencing record retail diesel prices and low inventory levels, indicating a tight global diesel market

blocks.text: A pump attendant fills vehicles with fuel at a gas station in Paco, Manila, on January 12, 2026, as prices are set to rise again.
Rappler
Refineries worldwide are operating at maximum capacity, with the US experiencing record retail diesel prices and low inventory levels, indicating a tight global diesel market

items: Diesel prices have surged to record highs in Europe and the US due to supply disruptions from conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, with European futures more than doubling since early 2026.
China's diesel exports have fluctuated, initially declining due to government restrictions but recovering significantly in August, impacting global supply dynamics.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

LONDON, UK – Diesel prices have rallied to record highs in Europe and the United States and are near record levels in Asia as wars in Iran and Ukraine disrupt supplies from major producers including Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, leaving few options to prevent further gains.

Diesel futures in Europe closed at an all-time high last week, having more than doubled from their level at the beginning of 2026, after supply disruptions spread to the Red Sea, where Saudi Arabia loads most of its diesel.
In Asia, diesel prices are elevated as a result of Middle East and Russian supply disruptions and close to record levels.

blocks.caption: Fuel prices rise again with big hike on September 22

blocks.text: Asian diesel prices eased from the March record high of more than $200 a barrel, hovering at around $180 a barrel on September 18.
Current levels are still twice the pre-war values.

China’s lower diesel exports in the aftermath of the Iran war likely tightened global supplies, as the country’s shipments declined by 26% in April-June from a year earlier due to a government decision to limit refined product exports.
But China’s diesel exports recovered to reach their highest in nearly 2.5 years in August at 320,000 bpd, resulting in lower domestic stocks.

The wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have damaged oil refineries in the region, and refineries elsewhere are working hard to make fuels. In the United States, for example, refineries operated at the highest level in eight years in late August, according to the International Energy Agency.

“A key issue is that many refineries around the world are already stretched to capacity,” the International Energy Agency said in a newsletter on Monday, September 21. “This leaves few available options to prevent a further tightening of supplies and higher prices in the coming months.”

Middle East diesel exports halved from March to August compared to a year earlier, averaging 800,000 barrels per day, according to shipping data from Kpler. The Middle East supplied nearly 41% of Europe’s diesel imports in 2025, Kpler data showed.

“Any further disruption to Red Sea flows risks tightening an already stretched global diesel market,” said Kpler analyst George Shaw, adding that global diesel markets remain vulnerable as refining capacity continues to be the key pinch point.
Russia banned diesel exports in July as Ukrainian drone attacks cut Russian refinery production.

Ukraine and Russia have continued attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure despite an announcement by US President Donald Trump last week that they had agreed to stop. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Sunday, September 20, he will meet with Trump in the coming days.

Russia, the world’s second-biggest diesel exporter after the United States, supplied significant volumes of diesel to Turkey and Brazil before the ban, prompting such importers to seek alternative supplies since then.

In Europe – historically a net importer of diesel – stocks at the key refining and storage hub of Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp were at their lowest level for this time of the year on September 10, according to data from Insights Global.
In the US, average retail diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time on record this month.

Inventories remain below normal seasonal levels, even as refiners have been running near full tilt. Although diesel stocks rose by roughly 600,000 barrels last week, at 96.97 million barrels they remain nearly 15% below the average for the last five years for the second week in September. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: Canada's privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a data breach at IDScan.net that potentially exposed details from millions of driver's licences and other kinds of government-issued…

image.caption: Canada's privacy commissioner is investigating a data security breach that exposed identification details from driver's licences and other government-issued ID. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Canada's privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a data breach at IDScan.net that potentially exposed details from millions of driver's licences and other kinds of government-issued identification from Canada and the U.S.
Privacy commissioner will look into IDScan.net breach involving Canada-issued driver's licences
IDScan.net provides identification verification software to several categories of businesses, from bars and casinos to car rental companies.

Earlier this month, the company published a public notice about a data security incident, stating that "an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud."

items: Woman flagged by ID scanner as nationwide 'public safety concern' after incident in Winnipeg bar
ID scan technology at Alcanna liquor stores collected too much data, says investigation

blocks.text: The company said it was notifying individuals who had potentially been affected and offered free credit monitoring services.

Two days before IDScan.net published its alert, the FBI confirmed it was looking into the reported theft of tens of millions of driver's licences belonging to people in the U.S. and Canada that were being sold on the dark net.
The bureau said it was “looking into the incident” but could not comment “due to the ongoing nature of the investigation.”
Unprecedented in size and scope
The breach could be one of the largest-ever exposures of government-issued identity documents in North America.
Zach Edwards, a threat researcher at the cybersecurity company Infoblox, told Reuters the incident was unprecedented in terms of its sweep.

"There's never been a breach of driver's licences at this scale," said Edwards, who added that he discovered his own license was part of it. Edwards said that the ongoing nature of the breach "means that this attack created legitimate national security risks for high-profile individuals."

Canada's Office of the Privacy Commissioner says it's examining the security safeguards IDScan.net had in place at the time of the breach and whether its actions to notify potentially affected Canadians were adequate.
The probe will also look at whether IDScan.net breached Canada’s federal private-sector privacy laws.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer wants judge to investigate juror's conduct
articles.summary: A lawyer for Lindsay Clancy is asking a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who wanted to convict the mother from Massachusetts of murder in the deaths of her three young children.

image.caption: Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington and his client Lindsay Clancy sit in a Plymouth, Mass., courtroom, earlier this month. Reddington is asking a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who wanted to convict the mother from Massachusetts of murder in the deaths of her three young children. (G

blocks.text: World·New
A lawyer for Lindsay Clancy is asking a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who wanted to convict the mother from Massachusetts of murder in the deaths of her three young children.
Judge urged to question juror about his cellphone use during deliberations and truthfulness on questionnaire
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

In a motion filed Friday but made public Monday, Clancy's lawyer asked the court to question juror Michael Desronvil about his alleged use of a cellphone during deliberations, his truthfulness on a questionnaire that prospective jurors filled out before the trial began and his truthfulness when jurors were questioned by the judge a day before the trial ended.

Among other things, lawyer Kevin Reddington asked the court to obtain a record of any calls or texts Desronvil made between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. on each day the jury deliberated. Phone use during deliberations is prohibited in the state.
Reddington is calling for the motion to be heard at the next scheduled hearing on Sept. 29.
Mistrial was declared

The judge declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after the jury insisted it couldn't reach a unanimous verdict, despite days of trying. Eleven of 12 jurors were ready to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that she was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids.
‘Impossible case’: Breaking down the Lindsay Clancy mistrial
But Desronvil sided with the prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing.
"I didn't have any doubts," Desronvil said in a statement released on the social platform X by his lawyer, Edward Paltzik.

The jury's foreperson had claimed in an earlier media interview that Desronvil had admitted having "reasonable doubt" about Clancy's guilt but wanted to convict her anyway. Desronvil said that wasn't true.

items: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror breaks silence, says he didn't have 'any doubts' of her guilt

blocks.text: "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he wrote. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing."
Juror hasn't been accused of wrongdoing
Desronvil hasn't been accused of any wrongdoing in connection with his service on the jury, though other jurors complained that he was inflexible in his opinion that Clancy was guilty.

Since the trial ended, Desronvil has been both publicly praised and scorned for his actions, and his personal life and past financial and legal problems have become the subject of scrutiny by the news media and amateur sleuths.

Among the public revelations: He had a restraining order against him at the time of jury selection and was facing eviction from his apartment due to over $12,000 US in unpaid rent. He also was accused of domestic violence in 2021, a charge that was later dismissed.

He also has been embraced by those who feel Clancy should be found guilty. A fundraiser to cover what organizers say are costs of "security, lawyers, and lost work" for Desronvil has raised nearly $375,000 US.
Not clear if Clancy will be tried again
Prosecutors have yet to say whether they plan on putting Clancy on trial again. She remains charged with murder and is in a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.

In another motion on Monday, another lawyer for Clancy, Martin Weinberg, asked the judge to take the unusual step of dismissing the criminal case, rather than putting on a new trial, on the grounds that a mistrial shouldn't have been declared in the first place.

Weinberg argued that the judge should have replaced the holdout juror with an alternate during the deliberations after a jury foreperson complained to the judge that one juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.
"Contrary to the court's stated believe at the time, it did have viable choices other than declaring a mistrial," Weinberg wrote.

items: How different would Lindsay Clancy's murder trial look if it happened in Canada?

blocks.text: That follows an earlier motion filed by Clancy's legal team arguing that Clancy shouldn't be tried a second time because prosecutors don't have enough evidence.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove either that Clancy did not have a mental disease or defect or that, despite having one, she retained the capacity to know what she was doing when she strangled her kids.
Reddington argued in Thursday's court filing that prosecutors proved neither.
A spokesperson for Plymouth County district attorney Timothy Cruz would not comment on the motions.

articles.title: Young people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’
articles.summary: Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go private Some of the most affluent areas of England have had the sharpest rises in the…

blocks.text: Some of the most affluent areas of England have had the sharpest rises in the proportion of young people claiming disability benefits for ADHD and autism since the pandemic, according to new research.

Claims for the personal independence payment (Pip) benefit for these health conditions were typically proportionally far higher in deprived areas with higher rates of poverty, low educational outcomes and insecure employment.
However, the fastest growth in ADHD and autism-related Pip claims has been in some of the country’s most prosperous areas such as Wokingham, Warwick, and parts of Hampshire and Surrey.

This trend probably reflects swifter access to ADHD and autism diagnoses in more affluent areas, say the researchers, in part highlighting the ability of wealthier families to skip long NHS waiting lists and pay privately for clinical diagnoses.

They say the relative gap in Pip claims between rich and poor areas is shrinking, with growth rates in wealthy places such as Runnymede in Surrey outstripping the likes of Blackpool and Stoke-on-Trent.

The research also found that Pip claim rates for ADHD and autism were higher among white people than other ethnic groups. This was reflected in lower than expected claims in ethnically diverse areas such as Newham and Brent, in London, and Leicester.

One of the sharpest rises was seen in leafy Surrey Heath (a 630% increase in Pip clams for autism and ADHD since 2019), while in contrast, the relatively deprived towns of Mansfield and Great Yarmouth saw 30% and 50% increases respectively.

The researchers say this shift is counterintuitive and unique to ADHD and autism. There is no evidence of similar trends in learning disability, depression, anxiety or physical conditions. Records from GPs show higher rates of new ADHD diagnosis in relatively affluent areas.

Sally Gainsbury, a senior policy analyst at the Nuffield Trust, which carried out the research, said the findings probably reflected “substantial inequality in access” to private and NHS diagnostic services, meaning “people with better resources and more support are often able to get to the front of the queue quicker”.

It may also reflect the ability of more privileged individuals to navigate a notoriously difficult and unpredictable Pip claims process, Gainsbury said. Obtaining a clinical diagnosis is likely to increase the chances of a successful Pip claim.

Pip is designed to help claimants with the extra costs of disability, such as energy, transport and food. It is not means-tested or linked to employment status and is paid to individuals whose condition impairs their ability to carry out everyday tasks.

About 205,000 16- to 24-year-olds received Pip for disabilities linked to ADHD or autism in April this year, a more than threefold increase since 2019, at a cost in 2025-26 of £1.36bn. The average Pip claim for this cohort was £8,800 a year.
after newsletter promotion

The sharp rise in numbers of young people claiming Pip and other disability benefits, particularly since the pandemic, has been at the centre of a political debate about the sustainability of working-age disability benefits spending, which is forecast to rise from £14bn in 2019 to £34bn in 2030.

The issue has become a culture war topic. Rightwing media and politicians have questioned the validity of Pip claims they say are the result of exaggerated mental health symptoms, and alleged overdiagnosis of neurodivergent conditions.

The Nuffield Trust research comes in advance of a government-commissioned report on mental health, autism and ADHD diagnoses. It is expected to recommend a “needs-based” system whereby overstretched NHS services target patients most acutely affected by ADHD, such as those who are at risk of self-harm or unable to work.

Led by Prof Peter Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst at University College London, the interim review published earlier this year concluded that the system forces children and adults to obtain a formal diagnosis in order to get support.

articles.title: Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges
articles.summary: Changes could save £33bn and result in average of four extra years of good health for people, report says The NHS in England could prevent 20,000 deaths and save £33bn a year by cutting red tape and…

blocks.text: The NHS in England could prevent 20,000 deaths and save £33bn a year by cutting red tape and boosting productivity, a report says.
Research by the Health Foundation found the health service has been held back for decades by excessive regulation, short-term planning and insufficient capability to deliver major change.
But rewiring the NHS, the world’s largest single healthcare system, by harnessing new technology, empowering staff and increasing capital investment could save both lives and money, it found.
There is “substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS”, which could result in up to four extra years of good health for people on average, the report said.
In terms of where deaths could be prevented, focusing on diagnosing cancer earlier and finding people with high blood pressure or conditions such as diabetes quicker would be key, it added.

The report called for a series of changes, such as releasing the NHS from unnecessary regulation, reporting and compliance tasks, as well as launching a “test-and-learn” approach to scaling up things that could improve productivity, such as use of artificial intelligence.

“Our analysis suggests that if the NHS in England achieved outcomes closer to the best-performing comparable health systems, without spending more each year, it could potentially result in 18,500–20,600 fewer deaths each year from treatable causes and 2.5 to 4.5 additional years that people spend in good health on average,” the report said.

Increasing NHS productivity is “sometimes … seen as exhorting hard-working staff to work even harder, in a system already under considerable strain” but this view must be challenged, it added. “At its heart, productivity means achieving better health outcomes from the resources available.”
The biggest issues affecting productivity included the “constant churn”, too many targets, and not enough focus on health outcomes.

Researchers also heard from staff how poor IT wasted clinical time, how limited estate and equipment constrained healthcare and how gaps in administrative support shifted additional work to clinicians.
While AI offered opportunities, the “NHS has repeatedly struggled to take advantage of the potential”, the report said.
Anita Charlesworth, report author and senior economic adviser at the Health Foundation, said: “This is mission critical for the NHS, which cannot simply keep doing more of the same.
“The problem is not a lack of committed and talented people or an absence of ideas; it is that the NHS is not set up to deliver sustained productivity growth.

“Our research points to a fundamental redesign of the operating conditions – not another disruptive reorganisation, but a reset to make improving productivity a defining focus for the NHS over the next decade and beyond.”

Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents and supports the health and care system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said he agreed more could be done to deliver further productivity gains but there were “big barriers” that would need to be addressed.

“Lack of capital investment has been a long-running drag on NHS productivity. More must be done to turn the tide on years of neglect … We also agree that a more streamlined, supportive regulatory system which encourages local autonomy and innovation will be vital for future progress.”

articles.title: Montreal city council adopts bylaw banning insults against police, municipal employees
articles.summary: Montreal city council has adopted a bylaw to ban people from insulting police officers and other municipal employees.

image.caption: Montreal's city hall building is seen here in a photo taken in November 2024. (Charles Contant/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
Montreal city council has adopted a bylaw to ban people from insulting police officers and other municipal employees.
Residents who insult city staff would face fines between $300 and $1,000 for a 1st offence
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 21, 2026 6:36 PM EDT | Last Updated: 10 minutes ago
The debate over the rule lasted over half an hour, with the Official Opposition saying the proposed bylaw was "half-baked." It was adopted with 35 voting in favour and 25 opposed.
"We are being asked to vote now and consult later," said Marie Plourde, leader of the Official Opposition.
Under the bylaw, residents who insult city staff would face fines between $300 and $1,000 for a first offence. Subsequent offences could result in fines up to $2,000.
City officials have not said when they will implement the bylaw.

Yves Francœur, head of the police brotherhood, has said his union's members have been pushing for such a bylaw for years. But lawyers and civil rights groups worry the bylaw could infringe on the constitutional right to freedom of expression.
Other municipalities in the province, including Quebec City, Laval, Longueuil and Sherbrooke, already have similar bylaws.

items: Police in Quebec municipalities issued thousands of fines for insulting officers

blocks.text: The Canadian Press reported in June that some of these municipalities have issued thousands of fines over the past six years.
"Giving the middle finger, it's not what will give you a ticket," Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said before the council meeting.
"Let's just be honest. There's bigger issues in terms of the attitude of some citizens."
City employees could refuse service
The new Montreal bylaw would ban insults, harassment, threats, abuse and intimidation, as well as offensive and aggressive behaviour.
It also includes provisions saying city employees could refuse to provide services to someone who misbehaves. However, the bylaw doesn't define what could be construed as an insult.
City councillor Carla Beauvais heavily criticized the administration for not providing clear definitions. She also questioned the lack of public consultations.

"A threat can be proven. An offensive word is felt. And how a person feels can vary from one person to another. So where does the offence begin? Where does permissible anger end? The text doesn't say," said Beauvais.
She cited various decisions from the Quebec City municipal court in which judges could not agree on what constitutes an insult, raising concerns that the rule will cause a backlog at the courthouse.
Citizens are concerned, councillor says

Opposition councillor Martine Musau Muele added that council was asked to vote on the rule without adequate information. She said the documents councillors received did not provide statistics and reports to support the need for the bylaw.
She also said the city did not conduct any risk assessment or prove that the measures under the Criminal Code are insufficient to deal with belligerent residents.

"Citizens are extremely concerned. People do not understand the reasoning of the administration. What led you to decide that today, with everything going on, that this is the most optimal move?" Muele said. "This is a draft, not a proposal."

items: Man who filmed himself insulting SPVM officer facing criminal defamation charges
Suspension of 4th Montreal officer in racism scandal renews calls for independent probe

blocks.text: The two councillors also raised concerns around giving police more powers while public trust is fragile.
In June, Montreal police disbanded a night patrol unit in the multicultural neighbourhood of Montréal-Nord over allegations of racism and misconduct.
Mayor acknowledges concerns

During council, Martinez Ferrada acknowledged that "there will be more questions around this bylaw in the coming months" but insisted the administration "needed to act." She said the administration would make reports publicly available.

She said she "understands the concerns," and "shares some of them." However, she said incidents of inappropriate behaviour have increased dramatically and are harming city employees, and making it more difficult to recruit new employees.
"We are simply saying that there is a line between challenging an institution and engaging in behaviour that is inappropriate toward the people who work for it," said the mayor.
"The thousands of women and men who work every day to serve Montreal have the right to protection from their employer, which is us."
She noted that women are most often the target of disrespectful behaviour and listed misogynistic insults she said employees commonly receive.

The debate around banning insults in Montreal resurfaced in March, after videos of a man insulting a police officer with misogynistic comments went viral. The man was charged in July with defamatory libel under the Criminal Code and had pleaded not guilty.
However, critics have said the bylaw could hinder de-escalation efforts and harm those who are victims of racial profiling, in crisis, or experiencing homelessness.

Four community organizations sent the mayor a letter on Sept. 17 expressing their concerns. These organizations include rights and freedom advocacy groups, a legal clinic and an anti-racism group based in the borough of Montréal-Nord, where the police patrol unit was disbanded.

items: Montreal police officers could start wearing body cameras within the next year, mayor says

blocks.text: "The proposed regulation does not merely prohibit violent behaviour or conduct that threatens physical integrity, which is already prohibited by the Criminal Code," the four organizations wrote in a joint letter. "It bans expressions that are not threatening simply because they are likely to cause discomfort, for example, 'offensive' behaviour."
They also argued the rules could be applied arbitrarily because it would be left to police officers' discretion to issue fines.
Another lawyer, Sibel Ataogul, has proposed offering free legal help to citizens contesting the bylaw.

articles.title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns
articles.summary: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID debacle The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.

The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.

The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.
A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.

The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.
External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.

The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.
Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.

At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.

The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.

“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”
Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.

“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”

The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.

The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.
The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

articles.title: Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion

image.caption: Prime Minister of Norway Jonas Gahr Støre, left, shakes hands with Prime Minister Mark Carney following a signing ceremony on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Sunday. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The Prime Minister of Norway says threats from Russia are part of the modern security picture and should be taken seriously.
Norway PM says Russian threat is real, welcomes closer defence ties with Canada
The prime minister of Norway says threats from Russia are part of the modern security picture and should be taken seriously.
In an interview with the CBC's Power & Politics, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told host David Cochrane "we are prepared, but not afraid" of a Russian incursion.
He said the threat is "real" and should be followed "very carefully," especially by countries closer to the Russian border — including Canada.
"Intelligence services of NATO countries are pointing to that threat. It is real. It's happening," Støre said.
The threat conversation came to the surface this week following a warning from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk that Russia is planning hybrid strikes on NATO territory.

Under this threat environment the Norwegian PM says regional groups must come together, welcoming Canada's recent move to seek membership in the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a collection of a few NATO nations whose mandate is to respond more quickly in a crisis.

The JEF was initially formed by the U.K., Netherlands, Nordic and Baltic countries, but Støre says it's now important to talk more closely with countries that he says, "share challenges and security risks," including Poland, Germany, Belgium and Canada.

items: Carney touts Arctic alliance with Norway during PM's visit to Ottawa, amid Russia threat
Russia is rattling NATO’s nerves, but how far will Moscow go?

blocks.text: Støre says the JEF is helpful in cases when issues may be too big for a country on its own or it's not up to the scale of Article 5 — the NATO clause that requires alliance members to defend any other member that's been attacked — telling Power & Politics that NATO allies are engaged in "sophisticated debate" over the threshold for Article 5 to be triggered.
With Russia struggling to reach its strategic objectives in Ukraine, it could be wanting to test Ukraine's partners, says Støre.
Incidents in Europe this summer have raised those alarm bells for NATO partners.

German authorities blamed Russia for a drone attack at an airport in central Germany in August while last week, Bulgarian authorities announced they're investigating a fire at a munitions storage facility operated by arms maker EMCO — whose weapons are used in Ukraine.
Norway looks to Canada as an Arctic partner

Following Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to Norway in March, both countries signed a strategic partnership committing to broadly expanding areas of co-operation — notably in the Arctic where both countries share a coastline with Russia.
"We see Canada very much part of the Northern sphere. We have the Atlantic between us, but we are Arctic states," Støre said.
With Russia not an ally in the Arctic, Canada and Norway must stay "very, very closely connected" to maintain order in the North.

items: Arctic militarization is a 'direct threat' to Russia, Kremlin says

blocks.text: In July, Carney chose to buy a dozen submarines from a European shipbuilder instead of a Korean firm, after a months-long, hotly contested bidding process. The chosen partnership involves a German company but partners with Norway, with the three nations collaborating to produce and maintain the submarines.
Inter-operability across submarines is a "major step" to increase Arctic security, Støre says, but also for industrial co-operation on Arctic research.
"That's why we need to work on our coast guards, that's why we need to work on our space ability to do surveillance. This is a very exciting theme between Norway and Canada."
Carney courts Europe

The Norwegian delegation's visit comes on the heels of Carney's address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, a meeting with the new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool, England, and a meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French territory 20 kilometres off the southern coast of Newfoundland.
As for EU "associate membership"?
Støre says he welcomes "deeper ties," with Canada but on a basis that's "real," and with "meaning."

items: EU chief says she wants Canada to become the bloc's 1st associate member

blocks.text: As Europe's most integrated non-EU country, Støre says Canada, the U.K. and Norway should work more closely together with the EU on new areas that require co-operation such as space, critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence.
"We can all benefit and not let that sink into bureaucracy and regulations that sometimes complicate things."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Mayson Maharaj is a producer for CBC's national television program Power & Politics and a writer for CBC's Parliament Hill bureau.

articles.title: U.S. shouldn't buy 'blood potash' from Belarus, Sask. premier says
articles.summary: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump posted on Monday that he is working on a potash deal with Belarus. (Alexander Quon/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source more of his country's fertilizer from Belarus.
Moe defends Sask. potash in post aimed at Trump's latest trade threat
"Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression," Moe said in a post on social media. "It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense."
Moe's post on Monday afternoon was a response to a Trump social media post from earlier that day.

"The United States is working on ​a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash ​from Belarus," Trump said on Truth Social. "The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for ​our Farmers and Ranchers."

items: Trump says U.S. working on deal to buy potash from Belarus instead of Canada

blocks.text: Potash is mainly used in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash production came from Canada and all of the country's 10 active potash mines are in Saskatchewan, according to Natural Resources Canada.
"More than 40 countries — Canada and its allies — have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine," Moe said in his social media post.

"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan — right here in North America?"

Nutrien Ltd., The Mosaic Company, Compass Minerals, and K+S Potash Canada are responsible for all of Canada's potash production. BHP is building the Jansen potash mine in Saskatchewan and expects to start commercial production in mid-2027.

items: Sask. is a potash and agriculture giant. So why is conflict in the Middle East a problem for farmers?

blocks.text: Nutrien is the largest potash fertilizer producer in Canada and one of the largest in the world. The Saskatoon-based company referred CBC to Fertilizer Canada when asked to comment on Trump's post.
U.S. farmers have used Canadian potash for decades, said Fertilizer Canada, an industry trade group, in an emailed statement to CBC News.
"Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter," the statement said.
"A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”
Last year, Nutrien announced plans to build a potash export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash., to handle expected growth in international demand for its fertilizer products.
The opposition NDP called Trump's social media post "infuriating" in a statement on Monday.
"He is looking at signing a deal with an authoritarian Russian satellite state that is supporting Putin’s brutal war against the people of Ukraine," the NDP statement said.
"This is a bad idea that will only hurt families and communities on both sides of the border."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeremy Warren is a reporter in Saskatoon. You can reach him at jeremy.warren@cbc.ca.

articles.title: UK: Man charged over suspected role in Rwanda genocide
articles.summary: The suspect has been accused of directing and inciting acts of murder and genocide carried out by others in Rwanda.

image.caption: Over 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate ethnic Hutus ⁠were killed in the 1994 genocide [FILE: April 4, 2014]Image: SIMON MAINA/AFP

blocks.text: UK authorities arrested and charged a man on Monday over alleged links to the Rwandan genocide, prosecutors and the London police said. It was the first arrest of its kind, although authorities have been pursuing the case for several years.
The 65-year-old man has been charged with one count of being an ancillary to genocide and six offenses of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, officials said.
"This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes," said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counterterror policing.

The Rwandan genocide took place in 1994, where over 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate ethnic Hutus ⁠were killed in a 100-day rampage, orchestrated and led by the Hutu ruling majority. Local officials and ordinary citizens were involved in the mass killing.
UK law allows prosecutors to bring charges for some international offenses, including genocide and crimes against humanity, even if the crimes were committed abroad.

It is the latest case of an arrest in Europe of someone linked to Rwanda's genocide. In July, a German-Rwandan national was arrested for charges of taking part in the genocide and killing one person himself.
Meanwhile, in the Netherlands, a man was sentenced to life in prison for having taken part in attacks on homes, including launching a grenade on sheltering Tutsi civilians.
Survivors remember Rwanda's 1994 genocide
Suspect underwent name change
UK's Metropolitan Police war crimes investigators opened the case against the suspect in 2019, following a request by the Rwandan government.
The 65-year-old is originally from Kigali but lived in London at the time of the arrest.
He reportedly entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998, according to Rwandan Justice Minister Tharcisse Karugarama.
After being granted British citizenship in 2004, the man underwent a name change, and two years later, he was arrested over his connection to the genocide.
His extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was ultimately halted by a British UK court in 2017.
The failed extradition prompted the Rwandan government to urge UK authorities to investigate the matter themselves.
Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's counterterror division, said the man is "alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others."
Authorities say investigations are ongoing for more suspects who are linked to the Rwandan genocide currently living in Britain.

articles.title: Halt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to say
articles.summary: At Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problem Ed Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation…

blocks.text: Ed Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI when he makes his keynote speech at the Liberal Democrat conference, accusing Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and “tech bros” to solve the problem.

When he addresses the faithful on the final day of the gathering in Brighton, the party leader will call for a global pause on super-intelligent AI, comparing it to a nuclear arms race that could result in technology that could “destroy us all”.

Davey is expected to lay out plans in his speech on Tuesday for a new international AI safety agency – modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and headquartered in the UK, after numerous warnings from AI researchers that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade. “We didn’t leave the atom bomb to a few billionaires to police themselves,” he will say.

Davey is expected to call for a new global movement to work together to protect humanity from the risks of super-intelligent AI, saying that the IAEA was built by nations “working together to control a technology that could destroy us all”, but warning that the future of AI is being decided by “a tiny number of the richest and most powerful in California and in Beijing” with no guardrails to slow down development.

“As liberals – we know that something as existential as nuclear weapons or climate change cannot be left in the hands of a powerful few. And so it must be with AI. We can’t leave it to Mark Zuckerberg, to Sam Altman, or to Elon Musk to save us,” Davey will say.
On Monday, the prime minister announced a new AI partnership with the US ahead of Trump’s address to the UN general assembly on Tuesday.
But Davey will say the plan “doesn’t come close to meeting the scale of this threat” and “only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros”.

It comes after the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, on Monday announced that the party proposed a big tech levy and promised to create a new online crime agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.

Wilkinson said the Lib Dems would properly regulate use of Meta’s smart glasses, which he called “perv goggles”, telling the conference that the glasses “are more than a benign piece of tech that provides a bit of fun” and that people – especially women – were being recorded without consent or warning. “This is becoming the new norm, because this government won’t stand up to big tech to protect our civil liberties,” he said.

On Sunday Davey set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.

blocks.caption: Ed Davey views the stands as he tours the exhibition hall during the conference in Brighton. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA

blocks.text: Davey defended himself in a series of interviews on Monday about complaints his party lacks vision, saying it was pointless to try to compete with the attention-grabbing ideas of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens.

“It’s a very noisy environment at the moment,” he told the BBC. “But let me tell you, some of the noise generated by the populists are things that divide our country, that are nasty, or that are just completely crazy. I don’t want to do that. I want to tell people that we have really well thought through policies that will cut their taxes.”

Asked if he would propose further tax cuts in the wake of the pledge to slash 10p from fuel duty for three months, Davey replied: “Absolutely.” These would, he said, be financed by higher economic growth due to the Lib Dem proposal to seek entry to the EU’s single market.

The Lib Dem leader did praise Burnham for wanting to reform adult social care, but told Sky News the “jury is out” on whether Burnham will deliver as prime minister. But Davey was positive about some of what Burnham has done.

“I think it’s good when other parties start talking about Liberal Democrat priorities,” he said. “We have led the debate on social care and carers because it’s so important for our health service. We’ve led the debate on political change because we need to change our political system, and Mr Burnham seems to be up for that.”

articles.title: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
articles.summary: Andy Burnham says he will urge Donald Trump to bring an end to conflict with Iran The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore…

blocks.text: The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.

The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.

Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world.

The ongoing turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government.

On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.

The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating.

“We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said.

The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result.

“Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump.

As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the United Nations general assembly.

The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak, with European leaders warning that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance.

Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology, and he will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.

Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending.

Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer.

They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy, with the prime minister expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, with the Jackdaw gas field likely to get the green light within weeks.

Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, with the Republicans facing a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings plummeting.
Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN general assembly, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday.

Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.

blocks.text: We're doing everything we can to curb domestic violence, says Chalmers

blocks.caption: Catie McLeod

blocks.text: Catie McLeod
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says the Albanese government is committed to doing “everything we can” to address to domestic violence, following a horrific weekend of violence in New South Wales.

Chalmers made the comments to ABC’s 7.30 program last night, after a mother allegedly fatally stabbed a child and wounded two others in the Blue Mountains and, separately, three other women were allegedly murdered inside their homes across the state.

Chalmers noted expert views that a lack of accessible housing played a role in domestic violence, along with the “magnitude” of misognystic content online. He also said front line staffing was crucial.

double quotation markI work closely with the prime minister and [women’s minister] Katy Gallagher and the relevant ministers to make sure that police and others get the resourcing they need, working with state governments.
Jim Chalmers says migration is necessary to support Australia’s ageing population, and can help the nation as birth rates tumble.

The three-yearly intergenerational report found that the declining birth rate meant more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time – the first time the report had made such a prediction.
Chalmers told 7.30 Australia’s birth rates were falling faster than anticipated just few years ago, because people are taking the decision to have smaller families later in life.
He said, in this context, “any objective observer would conclude that we need responsible levels of migration” to support the ageing population:

double quotation markMigration is a force for good in our economy and in our society. We will continue to make the case for getting that net overseas migration down in the most responsible way, that balances all of the key considerations in our economy and in local communities.

His comments come after the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, last week unveiled long-awaited changes to immigration rules, promising to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) to 245,000 this financial year, and 225,000 in 2027-28.
The City of Sydney has banned smart glasses
The City of Sydney has banned smart glasses in all its pools, libraries, gyms, childcare centres and town halls.
The council agreed to update signage and guidance to prevent people wearing the glasses in community facilities, due to growing privacy and harassment concerns.
In a statement, Greens councillor Matthew Thompson said his motion included exemptions for those who use the glasses as accessibility devices, including those with vision and hearing loss.
He urged the federal government to do more to regulate the glasses and prevent their misuse, saying that:

double quotation markOverseas we’re seeing women being targeted and harassed in public and recorded without their consent. We don’t want what’s happening in the US to happen here. That’s why we’re banning smart glasses and other wearable recording devices from all of our pools, gyms, childcare [centres], libraries and other council spaces. Cheap wearable devices like smart glasses are already flooding the market. But instead of stopping this problem, the federal Labor government has dumped it on to councils to sort out. We need an import ban on these cheap, intrusive devices until we have stronger privacy protections and clear standards implemented nationally.

Last week, Sydney’s Canterbury-Bankstown council introduced its own restrictions on the technology. Its mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.
In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools. Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says the Albanese government is committed to doing “everything we can” to address to domestic violence after a weekend of violence in New South Wales. More coming up.

articles.title: Crown withdraws criminal charges against former Cricket Canada CEO Salman Khan
articles.summary: Criminal charges were dropped Monday against former Cricket Canada CEO Salman Khan, who was accused of misappropriating $200,000 from the Calgary and District Cricket League.

image.caption: All charges have been withdrawn against former CEO of Cricket Canada, Salman Khan. (Mohit Kumar/Facebook)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
Criminal charges were dropped Monday against former Cricket Canada CEO Salman Khan, who was accused of misappropriating $200,000 from the Calgary and District Cricket League.
Salman Khan faced charges of fraud and theft over $5,000
Criminal charges were dropped Monday against a former Cricket Canada CEO who was accused of misappropriating $200,000 from the Calgary and District Cricket League.
Salman Khan Shahzad (a.k.a. Salman Khan), 47, was charged with counts of fraud over $5,000 and theft over $5,000 in March 2025 stemming from alleged illegal activity between 2014 and 2016.
On Monday morning, which was supposed to be Day 1 of Khan’s trial, prosecutor Petter Hurich appeared in a Calgary courtroom and withdrew the charges.
Syed Wajahat Ali, the league’s former treasurer, was accused of the same offences and says his charges were withdrawn earlier this year.
'This was the right result'

In a statement provided to CBC News, the Crown Prosecution Service said prosecutors have “an ongoing obligation to review all available admissible evidence to ensure the matter continues to meet the standard for prosecution.”
“In this file, the Crown prosecutor determined there was insufficient evidence to proceed to trial.”

items: Cricket Canada CEO says charges of theft and fraud are 'completely false'

blocks.text: Defence lawyer Jim Lutz said his client was “greatly relieved” with Monday’s development.
“This was the right result in law for Khan,” said Lutz.

“We came to this conclusion after almost a year’s worth of work on this file, critically evaluating the evidence. My client is extremely grateful the Crown took the time to thoroughly review this file.”
Cricket Canada termination
Cricket Canada terminated Khan in December 2025, nine months after Calgary police announced the charges following a board-led investigation.

“The dismissal stems from Mr. Khan’s failure to disclose prior criminal charges — an act that constituted a serious breach of trust — along with violations of organizational bylaws related to his contract,” said the board in a statement posted to the Cricket Canada website.

According to reporting by CBC's the fifth estate, Khan's Cricket Canada contract had a provision that stated he is entitled to his full term pay if he's fired for any reason other than a criminal conviction related to his position as CEO.
Khan is reportedly fighting for Cricket Canada to honour his contract and pay out the remaining $475,000.
CBC News has reached out to Cricket Canada for comment.
The investigation
Calgary police launched its investigation after concerns were flagged during a 2017 audit of the league’s financial records, conducted by the newly appointed president.

When police announced the charges last year, investigators alleged Khan and Ali misappropriated funds through cheque payments to construction businesses and contractors connected to the former president and treasurer.
Police said at the time that payments were allegedly made for repairs and upgrades to the league clubhouse and grounds for work that was either never completed or poorly done using inferior products.
Match fixing allegations
Khan was also named in connection with a fifth estate investigation into allegations that the Bishnoi gang — run from an India prison by leader Lawrence Bishnoi — has influence over Cricket Canada.

items: Threats, corruption and intimidation: Is the Bishnoi gang calling shots at Cricket Canada?
'We will rule in CANADA': Letter from Bishnoi gang to police disclosed to CBC News

blocks.text: The fifth estate obtained audio from a former Cricket Canada head coach claiming he was asked to fix parts of matches by then-CEO Khan and two other former leaders within the organization.
In a lengthy email provided to CBC News, Khan said he categorically denies "any involvement in spot fixing, session fixing, betting or influencing team selection for improper purposes."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Families of Air India bombing victims 'utterly shocked' to learn investigation is inactive
articles.summary: CBC News has learned that the families of the Air India bombing victims have sent letters to the RCMP and the Prime Minister expressing their dismay that the investigation into the crash is now…

image.caption: A memorial for the Air India bombing is seen in Vancouver in June 2025. The families of the victims say the RCMP has told them the investigation into the bombing is inactive. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

CBC News has learned that the families of the Air India bombing victims have sent letters to the RCMP and the Prime Minister expressing their dismay that the investigation into the crash is now inactive.
Families were told by RCMP they had no more information to pursue in the case
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 21, 2026 3:57 PM EDT | Last Updated: 25 minutes ago

The RCMP held a meeting in Toronto on Sept. 12, according to letters viewed by CBC News, where the families say they were told there is no further information to pursue in the case. CBC News has reached out to the RCMP for confirmation and not yet heard back, but has spoken with several people who say they attended the meeting.
Sanjay Lazar, who lost his parents and sister on the 1985 flight bombing, said the families had no idea what was coming in the meeting they'd been called to in a hotel near the Toronto airport.

"They said that we don't have any more leads. We cannot pursue and we need to identify significant persons in this. And therefore we are going to start, well, winding down," Lazar told CBC News in an interview Monday.
"You can't just abandon the whole investigation purely because you feel you've reached a dead end."

On June 23, 1985, Air India Flight 182 took off from Toronto to Mumbai with stops in Montreal, London, England, and New Delhi. A bomb in a suitcase in the hold exploded, and the plane broke apart over the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Ireland.

All 329 people on board were killed, most of whom were Canadian citizens. The bombings are considered the worst mass murder in Canadian history. Investigations and a public inquiry exposed major Canadian intelligence and security failures.

Only one person was ever convicted in connection with the bombing: bomb-maker Inderjit Singh Reyat. He served his 30-year sentence and was released in 2016. Two other men were tried and acquitted in 2005. One of those men, Ripudaman Singh Malik, was shot and killed in 2022. Another suspect was killed in India in 1992.

items: A timeline of the Air India case, from the bombings to the death of an old suspect

blocks.text: Rob Alexander, who lost his father in the explosion, says the meeting was "long overdue," noting it had been many years since the RCMP spoke with the families. He told CBC News about 40 or 50 family members were in attendance Sept. 12, and another 20 or so connected through Zoom.

"They told us that because they felt they had exhausted most of the strings of evidence that they had been following over the years, they were kind of parking the investigation and kind of going inactive," Alexander said.
"And the family members were utterly shocked.

"We know it's been a long time, and things get exhausted and people die off and we get that. But to shelve the whole thing and make it inactive, it is a big slap in the face to the memories of the people that we lost."
'Utter shock and horror'

The letter from the RCMP addressed to "The Families of the victims of Air India Flight 182, 1985," which has been viewed by CBC News, invited family members to attend the meeting that would "provide an update on the current status of the Air India Flight 182 investigation, including an outline of future steps."
"We recognize that this continues to be a deeply personal and difficult experience, and we are committed to keeping you informed and supported," reads the invitation.
Sudha Berry, whose 16-year-old brother Sharad was killed, wrote a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and several other ministers and RCMP officials to express her family's "utter dismay."

"The decision took most of the families of the passengers that perished on that flight completely by surprise. We have waited patiently for 41 years for the RCMP to deliver justice in the names of those we lost," Berry wrote.
"The decision is a betrayal of the families' trust and a complete dereliction of the RCMP's duty towards them."
Lazar wrote in a letter to the RCMP commissioner that he was "struck down by lightning" and experienced "utter shock and horror" when RCMP informed the families the investigation is inactive.
"Many family members were distraught at hearing this," Lazar wrote in the letter dated Sept. 17 and obtained by CBC News.

He described the Sept. 12 meeting as "a gut wrenching kick in my abdomen, and it brought back dark memories for me, of that young 17-year-old kid who watched bodies & body parts coming into Cork for almost 25 days on that rainy month of June."

Bob Rae, Canada’s former United Nations ambassador who did a preliminary Air India inquiry in 2005, told CBC News it was wrong for the RCMP to consider winding down the investigation and that he's "deeply troubled" by their approach.
"It's not a smart approach or a smart move," Rae said, adding it's not going to help Canada's reputation in India.
"This is the most serious mass crime committed in Canadian history."

articles.title: Infantino says he is open to talks over Fifa reform
articles.summary: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates. shifting tone as he seeks support to stay on.

blocks.text: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform.
In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino explains the independent process would "recommend potential improvements".
Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened".
This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash.

In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you", and says the consultation will be with confederations, member associations and "relevant stakeholders".
He insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!"

His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not."
Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be."
He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together".

Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves.
FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.
Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football.
"We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association," he adds in the letter.
"What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided.

"The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead."

Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE.
Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.
Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents.
Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.

Having defiantly clung to power for weeks amid an unprecedented rebellion over his presidency, this is a significant change in tone from Infantino - and the first sign that he may feel he has no choice but to compromise if he is to win another re-election in March.
On 15 October, the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since this crisis began, and Infantino will no doubt hope that this relieves some of the pressure he is under.
But even if he is prepared to accept some changes to the way Fifa is run, will that be enough to win over some of those that have turned against him?

As well as wanting him to step down, many of Infantino's critics want an overhaul of Fifa's governance, with curbs on the president's power (such as a maximum of a single term in office), more separation between the president and the Fifa administration, greater emphasis on human rights and sustainability, and the redistribution of Fifa's cash reserves.
It will be fascinating to see if Infantino is prepared to accept such changes if it means staying in power.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre surprised many when he announced at a rally on Sunday that Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis will be the party's candidate in Brantford-Brant South.

In a Facebook post, Carrol said that on Sunday he learned that "one candidate has been appointed rather than selected through the nomination contest that so many of us had been preparing for. I wish Kevin Davis well, but I would be less than honest if I said I wasn't deeply disappointed."

Carrol said "The grassroots tradition of this party is what drew me to it nearly two decades ago, and I've spent those years helping build it here… knocking on doors, getting memberships, raising money, supporting our candidates and trusting local members to make good choices. articles.title: Converse apologizes, pulls ad that critics say evokes KKK and lynching imagery
articles.summary: After intense backlash that included a U.S. congressman, several celebrities, marketing experts and a wide swath of the internet, Converse has pulled the sneaker ad critics have accused of evoking Ku…

image.caption: Converse shoes are seen in this 2022 file photo. Converse, a brand owned by Nike, has apologized and pulled a new ad after criticism the ad's imagery resembled a lynching. (Andrew Kelly/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

After intense backlash that included a U.S. congressman, several celebrities, marketing experts and a wide swath of the internet, Converse has pulled the sneaker ad critics have accused of evoking Ku Klux Klan imagery, and apologized.
Converse says it understands ad is 'deeply upsetting' in apology
It's been called disgusting, harrowing and racist.

Now, after intense backlash that included a U.S. congressman, several celebrities, marketing experts and a wide swath of the internet, Converse has pulled the sneaker ad critics have accused of evoking Ku Klux Klan imagery, and apologized.
"We're sorry," Converse, which is owned by Nike, said in a statement to CBC News Monday.
"We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong," Converse continued in the statement that was first released Friday.
"We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better."

The ad, posted on social media Sept. 3, showed a model — KPop singer Karina — holding a pair of Chuck 70 X high top sneakers. Many people have pointed out online that the lighting on Karina's skirt, which created a white triangle, resembles a KKK hood. And the placement of the sneakers made them look like dangling feet, evoking for many a lynching victim.
"That's a lynching, yes?" actor Yvette Nicole Brown wrote on Threads Thursday.
U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, in a lengthy statement Friday, called the ad "racist, reckless and deeply offensive."
"Nike and Converse, what the hell were you thinking?" he said.

Carter called on the companies to explain how the ad was approved, adding that an apology isn't enough. In doing so, he joined the chorus of other critics who allege that the imagery was obvious and wouldn't simply get missed without several levels of corporate failures.
"Do not insult our intelligence by dismissing this as an unfortunate misunderstanding. An advertising campaign does not just appear," he said.
"It is conceived, photographed, reviewed, approved and distributed. At every stage, someone had the opportunity — and the responsibility — to say no."
Hanging deaths evoke lynching history
Converse's ad comes as the Southern U.S. grapples with several recent deaths involving Black people found hanging from trees.

Over the past two years, about a half-dozen Black women and men have been found hanged across the South. Police in some of those cases quickly deemed them suicides — often eliciting historically grounded skepticism when investigators provided limited evidence ruling out foul play.

As the Associated Press points out, for many Black people, the imagery of a rope and noose evokes the legacy of lynching and vigilante violence against Black people in the U.S. and brings with it deep pain and trauma.

items: Sydney Sweeney's 'sexualized' sports betting ad slammed by Canadian athletes
Montreal police allegedly cut locs from people's hair. Here's the anti-Black history behind that

blocks.text: Converse's "apology doesn't undo what got past legal, marketing, and leadership at every step," Lee Merritt, a civil rights attorney based in Texas, posted on Instagram Friday.
"This wasn't hidden. It was styled, lit, and approved by a creative team. Someone signed off on this."

Several media outlets have reported that a second Converse ad posted by the brand's Malaysia Instagram account earlier this month depicted a man climbing a wooden ladder to reach a pair of shoes seen dangling from a tree, which critics have also said evoke lynching imagery.
CBC News has seen copies of images of the ad shared on social media, but not the original, so can't yet confirm. CBC has reached out to Converse for clarity on the second ad and not yet heard back.
Racially insensitive ads in the spotlight
Several companies and brands have come under fire lately for racially insensitive products and campaigns.

Last month, for instance, retailer Target pulled a children's Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

Last year, American Eagle and actor Sydney Sweeney faced backlash for an ad campaign that was criticized for promoting white standards of beauty at best, and eugenics at worst. In the ad, Sweeney makes a play on words between jeans (the clothing item) and genes (the genetic material).

Gucci apologized in 2019 for a sweater accused of resembling blackface. In 2018, H&M apologized for its image of a Black boy in a sweatshirt that said "coolest monkey in the jungle." The year before, Dove said it "missed the mark" for a body wash commercial in which a Black woman lifts her shirt to reveal a white woman underneath.
