articles.title: Weather tracker: Japanese islands brace for Dujuan to become a typhoon again
articles.summary:
Storm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quiet

Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding…

blocks.text: Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back into a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph.

Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands.

Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week.

The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto.

South-west Europe may get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.

articles.title: Three arrested in South Africa over one of nine women's bodies found
articles.summary: The body of Jabulile Ntimba was the ninth to be found recently in an area east of Johannesburg.

blocks.text: Three suspects have been detained in South Africa in connection with the murder of a woman in an area east of Johannesburg – the last of nine recent cases in that region that has shone a spotlight on the level of violence against women in the country.
Under pressure to solve the spate of murders which has involved victims' bodies being dumped on a roadside, police have described the arrests of the three – a man and two women - as a "breakthrough".
Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice".
The three suspects are due in court on Monday morning.
Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday.

Several of the recent victims were discovered partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.

Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

blocks.caption: Plans for a highway toll (Maut) in Germany have so far failed Image: Bernd Wüstneck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.

Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.
Both of them deny the charges made against them.
What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?

The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.

Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.
The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.
But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.
The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.
Jail sentences possible
The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.
If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.

articles.title: Police officer and man injured in shooting outside Belleville, Ont., synagogue
articles.summary: A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized…

image.caption: Belleville police officers stand outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue Sunday night. The incident occurred on the street in front of the synagogue. Last night, the synagogue was taped off as part of the crime scene. (CBC)

blocks.text: Canada

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.
Shooting occurred as members of Jewish community gathered for Yom Kippur

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in the southern Ontario community of Belleville as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.

Ontario's Special Investigations Unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, about 175 kilometres east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man around 7:10 p.m. and that both were taken to a hospital.

Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.
The Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.

items: 'Canada's civic compact is failing Jewish Canadians,' Carney says in speech addressing antisemitism

blocks.text: Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was underway.

I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur.

My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to…—fordnation
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.

"I'm disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur," Ford said in a post on social media.
Ford said Jewish people "have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear" and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
"My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones," Ford said.
Surge in antisemitism
York Regional Police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Sunday's shooting comes months after Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.

Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.

Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

articles.title: Merz insists he will stay as German chancellor despite heavy losses in state elections – Europe live
articles.summary:
CDU suffered heavy losses in two regional elections, including in home state of former leader Angela Merkel, where it polled just 4.9%

Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 11m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where we’ll start in Germany after a bruising night for Friedrich Merz’s party.

The German chancellor is staring down pressure over his leadership and authority after the CDU suffered heavy losses in two regional elections. For the first time in 77 years, it’s failed to enter a state parliament, in the former East German state of Mecklenburg- Vorpommern.
This was the home state of former CDU chancellor Angela Merkel; the party there last night pulled just 4.9% of the vote, losing more than half of its support.

Many of its voters have flocked to Alternative for Germany (AfD). The far-right, anti-migrant party gained 38% of the vote, doubling its share to now become the largest party in the state. This result comes just a fortnight after AfD romped to a majority in Saxony-Anhalt.
Merz called it a “disaster” last night in a public address, but vowed to stay the course and press on with his government’s reforms.

articles.title: Pakistan says strikes in Afghanistan killed '28 terrorists'
articles.summary: The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were struck overnight. Pakistan said 28 militants were killed, Afghanistan said three civilians died. This follows soon after an attack on police in…

image.caption: Taliban officials accused Pakistan of targeting civiliansImage: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistan's Ministry of Information described as suicide bomber training facilities.
It was the first Pakistani strike of its kind on Afghan territory since June, and followed soon after an attack targeting Pakistani police across the border in Kohat.
The uneasy neighbors reported seemingly conflicting casualty tolls.
What were the conflicting accounts on the strikes?
Pakistan's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting claimed online that the attacks had targeted terrorist training sites in Afghanistan with "precision and accuracy."

"Three targets were destroyed with precision including a Suicide Bombers training markaz [station], killing 28 terrorists alongside multiple suicide bombers. Large quantities of weapons and ammunition ... were also destroyed," the Ministry said.
The Taliban government in Kabul, meanwhile, claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes."
Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces.

Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded.
He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed.
Neither side's assertions on the details of and casualties from the strikes could be immediately verified.

blocks.caption: The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calmImage: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan

The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border.
At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack.
Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack.
The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict
Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February.
Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan, following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan.
Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people.
Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June.
Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory.
Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas.
The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem.
Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war?

articles.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
articles.summary: German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on…

image.caption: Germany's auto industry is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the countryImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.
Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.

Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?

Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.
"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."

Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.
Labor costs too high in Germany?
Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.
Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a reportpublished by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.
To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.
The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.
It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."
Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.

Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.

The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.
IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.
VW is bringing out the axe
Can longer working hours save jobs?
The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.
The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.
"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.

Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.
On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.
"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.
How can Germany's auto industry recover?
Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.
"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.

He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.
"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.
At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.
Could VW's Osnabrück car plant pivot to arms production?
Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.
"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.
And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.

"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."

articles.title: US proposes AI safety mechanism in talks with China
articles.summary: US Treasury chief Scott Bessent said there had been "successful" talks with China on trade and AI. The talks come amid growing fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

image.caption: Hopes of finding common ground on concerns over AI safety comes amid fierce competition between the two countriesImage: Bai Xueqi/Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Top officials fro the United States and China have discussed a communication mechanism dealing with AI concerns between the two countries.
The talks on Sunday evening come ahead of a summit this week between US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping and amid growing fears that AI poses an existential threat to humanity.
The discussion with a team led by China's Vice Premier He Lifeng also involved top US trade official Jamieson Greer and took place at JPMorgan Chase's New York headquarters.
What is AI's biggest risk: Speed or autonomy?
What did US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent say about the AI talks with China?
"We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters.
Bessent said the delegations spoke about a mechanism to communicate about AI issues, calling it the "US-China AI dialogue."
"The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries," Bessent said.

The US Treasury chief said that these notifications would be for potential "incidents" or an instance "that rises up to a national security level from AI," he said, adding that both sides have agreed to meet again.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said at the conclusion of the talks.
What has been reported in China?
Chinese state news agency Xinhua described the talks as "candid, in-depth, and constructive" on Monday.

"The two sides engaged in... discussions on key economic and trade issues of mutual interest, such as implementing the consensus from previous consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment," Xinhua reported in a brief readout.
Xinhua added that Chinese and US officials also held a dialogue on "issues related to AI", with no further details provided.
AI fear machine?
Concern over the threat posed by AI
In recent weeks, leading AI firms have warned of the threat posed by unbridled AI development and the pace at which these threats could become a reality.
They have begun working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry amid rising fears about its dangers.

Late in August, more than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats.

That came after it emerged that OpenAI models had gone rogue and had hacked into a digital repository of AI technology. Anthropic conducted investigations to see if its own models had carried out similar attacks and found three incidents in which a Claude model and later identified a fourth incident.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?
AI experts sound the alarm
Earlier this month, researcher Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI companies were "gambling with our lives."
Former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed his concerns, warning that "AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."
Trump has dismissed calls to better curb AI's development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy."
Trump's stance has been applauded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose chipmaking company powers the vast majority of AI systems. Huang thanked the US president for "seeing through" the warnings on AI.

articles.title: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance
articles.summary: The groups have been active in Ethiopia's most populous regions for years and now say they will work together.

blocks.text: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa and push for a transitional administration.

The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival.
The groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction, and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration.
Federal authorities have not yet responded.
Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country.
There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions.
An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement.
Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Ogaden, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz – making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states.
Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces during the Tigray war.
It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm.
The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018.
The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea.
Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities".
"Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July.

The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties.
The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results.
The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll.

Search and rescue authorities in the southern state of Kerala found three more dead bodies on Monday morning, taking the death toll from a flash flood to at least five.

Six people were swept away on Sunday evening in the scenic town of Nilambur when the Kottapuzha River rose due to rainfall higher up in the landscape, local media reported. The search for the sixth person is still on.
Floods and rain-triggered landslides are a common occurrence in Kerala during the monsoon months, between June and November.
The state's Chief Minister VD Satheesan is set to arrive in the town shortly.
Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued orange alerts for six districts in the state on Monday morning, warning of more downpour.

An orange alert is the second highest in IMD's four-stage color-coded system, sitting just below the red warning. It tells local authorities and residents to 'be prepared' for heavy to very heavy rainfall in the region.

articles.title: Sydney policeman allegedly disguised himself as Uber Eats rider before murders
articles.summary: Beaumont Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the 2024 murder of his ex-partner and his new boyfriend.

blocks.text: A former police officer accused of using his work gun to kill a Sydney couple was driven by a "jealous infatuation" with his ex, a court has heard.
Beaumont Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two charges of domestic violence-related murder and one of aggravated break and enter.

Prosecutors allege Lamarre-Condon shot his ex-partner, 26-year-old TV presenter Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies, a 29-year-old Qantas flight attendant, at a home in the Sydney suburb of Paddington in 2024.
The couple's bodies were found in a rural area 200km away, hidden in surfboard bags. The trial is expected to run for three months.
In his opening address on Monday, prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC described how Lamarre-Condon had developed an "obsessive and jealous infatuation" with Baird after a brief romantic relationship.
It manifested itself in a "range of compulsive behaviour", Hatfield said, which escalated when Baird ended all contact in November 2023.
The barrister said Lamarre-Condon used a friend's phone to message Baird and claim he had cancer, stalked his ex-lover, and tampered with his car in the weeks after their break-up.

On the day of the alleged murders, Lamarre-Condon had set his alarm for 04.30 local time, Hatfield claimed, and sent a text to a friend which read: "I'll try to call you tonight and update you... there's no sign I'm doing it".

Lamarre-Condon then switched to a burner phone, picked up a rental car and waited outside Baird's home for three hours dressed as an Uber driver, the prosecution alleged. He had previously bought a surfboard bag to dispose of Baird's body, Hatfield said.

After entering Baird's home with a key he had previously obtained, Lamarre-Condon shot Baird in the kitchen and then killed Davies in the bedroom as he was trying to call emergency services for help, the court was told.
Hatfield said that the accused had planned Baird's murder, and killed Davies so as to "eliminate him as a witness".
In the hours and days after the alleged killings, Lamarre-Condon tried to cover up the murder, Hatfield said, including sending messages from Baird's mobile phone.
The aggravated break and enter charge that Lamarre-Condon is facing refers to an incident in August 2023 where it's alleged he broke into Baird's home and stole his phone and wallet.
Hatfield also told the court that Lamarre-Condon had earlier offered to plead guilty to a single charge of manslaughter relating to Baird's death but this was rejected.
Police were first alerted to the alleged murders after bloodied items belonging to Baird and Davies were found in a bin in Sydney's south.
Later that week, Lamarre-Condon handed himself in to a police station and was charged.
Eight days after the alleged killings took place, authorities found the couple's bodies.
Lamarre-Condon was sacked by New South Wales Police in the weeks after he was charged with the alleged murders.

Before the opening address on Monday, a 15-member jury was selected, with the judge, Justice Natalie Adams, explaining that three extra people were chosen - a jury is typically made up of 12 people - as a contingency for sickness and other unforeseen circumstances.

articles.title: Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, dies aged 27
articles.summary: His family asked for privacy during a "very difficult and painful time" following the model's death.

blocks.text: Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, has died at the age of 27.
Gerber, a model, passed away at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to records filed by the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. The cause of death was not listed.
Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US news partner CBS: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."
Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his runway debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.
He went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta.
His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.
In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use.

In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do."
And in this month's American Vogue, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone.
"I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help."

Gerber had previously spoken of his close relationship with his family, including sister Kaia, who he appeared alongside in a campaign for Calvin Klein in 2018, and whose name he had tattooed on his arm.
He told People Magazine that year: "We're a close family, especially me and my sister, so it's definitely cool.
"We get to travel together half of the time, so it makes it a lot less lonely."
Gerber also starred alongside his mother in Pepsi's 2018 Super Bowl commercial, 26 years after Crawford first appeared in her famous 1992 advertisement for the brand.
"We're a really tight family, so it was just like going to work with one of your friends. It was so fun, and easy," he told People Magazine at the time.
In July, Crawford shared two childhood photographs of her son on Instagram to mark his 27th birthday.
"I'm so proud of the man you've become, but I'll always see you as my little boy! Love you," she wrote.

articles.title: 'No surprises' as results emerge in Russian parliamentary election
articles.summary: Preliminary results suggest that Kremlin-backed United Russia is on course to retain its constitutional majority.

blocks.text: Preliminary results from Russia's elections suggest that the party backed by President Vladimir Putin, United Russia, will maintain its grip on parliament.
The outcome comes as no surprise, according to the BBC's Russia editor, Steve Rosenberg, who has been following the elections from Moscow.
The vote comes after more than four and a half years of war against Ukraine, a conflict which has seen huge battlefield losses for the Russian army and sparked economic hardship.
The only anti-war party, Yabloko, was removed the ballot in the run-up to polling day – although some candidates remained in some constituencies.

articles.title: 'Far from their best' to 'a joy to watch' - ranking Premier League teams' start to season
articles.summary: Five matches into the league season, which teams in the Premier League have impressed so far and who have disappointed?

blocks.text: There is now a three-week international break with no Premier League games until 10 October.
We are five matches into the league season and there is a long way to go in the campaign, but which teams have impressed so far and who have disappointed?
You can have your say in the comments at the bottom of the page.
Arsenal: Solid start to their title defence until they were ripped apart by Brighton having survived a penalty scare at Sunderland. 7
Aston Villa: Signs they are beginning to move in the right direction after losing so many key players during the transfer window. 6
Bournemouth: If games lasted 80 minutes the Cherries would be near the top of the table. Need to cut out conceding so late. 6
Brentford: Demolished Spurs and Chelsea without fuss during a highly impressive unbeaten start. Can they keep it up and challenge for Europe? 8
Brighton: Kings of entertainment after hitting 16 goals in five top-flight games, including three against champions Arsenal. A joy to watch. 9
Chelsea: After a strong start under Xabi Alonso, the Blues have lost two of their past three - and were picked apart by Brentford. Are they really moving in the right direction? 6
Coventry City: You could hear the sighs of relief in the away end at Nottingham Forest on Saturday. Will Frank Lampard's side kick on after that win? 6
Crystal Palace: Room for improvement after one win and three defeats. 5
Everton: Despite a transfer window to forget, David Moyes has made the Toffees hard to beat. 6

Fulham: Decent draws against Liverpool and Manchester United but need a win. Ipswich (away) followed by Hull (home), Coventry (away) and Crystal Palace (home) offer hope when they return from the international break. 5
Hull City: To have eight points from a tough opening five fixtures is an excellent return, including beating Manchester United and drawing with Aston Villa and Chelsea. 8
Ipswich Town: Defensively vulnerable but two late winners, against Sunderland and Crystal Palace, have earned them six points and shown their fighting spirit. 5
Leeds United: Fifth in the league, unbeaten and with the joint-best defensive record. They showed what they are capable of with a superb 4-1 win over Newcastle. 7
Liverpool: Unbeaten but have been far from their best. Three clean sheets in their past three games, but more is expected from Andoni Iraola's side. 6

Manchester City: Five league games, five victories. Managed to win at Manchester United despite going down to 10 men midway through the first half. With Erling Haaland already top scorer, City fans will expect a real push to win the league. 9

Manchester United: Disappointing performances to lose at Hull and draw at a Fulham side who were bottom of the league. Their only win so far came against Ipswich and they were denied a victory at Everton by a late equaliser. 4

Newcastle United: A mixed bag under new manager Matthias Jaissle. They impressed in a draw against Liverpool, won comfortably at Tottenham, but were also terrible in a loss at Leeds, although they responded well to beat Hull. 6

Nottingham Forest: Their best results have come away, drawing at Liverpool and winning at Aston Villa. But their home form will be a huge worry - yet to score a goal and with only one point from three matches at the City Ground. 5

Sunderland: After coming seventh in 2025-26, Sunderland fans will have wanted a better start to this season. The Black Cats gave good accounts of themselves against Arsenal and Manchester City, but lost both matches. 5

Tottenham Hotspur: After spending more than £300m in the summer, Spurs have been poor, failing to score in their opening four league matches. Supporters will be demanding an instant improvement after the international break. 2

articles.title: Japan: Typhoon Dujuan sparks flood, landslide warnings
articles.summary: At least 275 flights have been canceled in Japan, which is in the middle of a five-day holiday. The storm could dump record levels of rain on the country.

image.caption: Parts of the Izu Islands and the Chiba prefecture, near Tokyo, already saw heavy rains this weekendImage: Takuya Matsumoto/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A powerful typhoon was nearing Japan's eastern coast on Monday, triggering warnings of floods and landslides and prompting hundreds of flights to be canceled.
Dujuan is forecast to pass close to the Tokyo metropolitan area later in the day.
What do we know about Typhoon Dujuan?
Typhoon Dujuan was packing winds at speeds of 144 kilometers (89 miles) per hour as it lingered some 110 kilometres from Hachijojima, one of Tokyo's most remote islands.
Parts of the Izu Islands and the Chiba prefecture near Tokyo already saw heavy rainfall over the weekend.
The ⁠Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has cautioned that weather conditions could worsen rapidly.
"The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain," the JMA said.

Authorities have also warned of a possibility of ⁠linear ​rain bands forming over central Japan and the Kanto region — which includes Tokyo and surrounding prefectures — that could raise the risk of rain-related disasters like flash floods and landslides.
Linear ‌bands cause heavy torrential rainfall ​over a narrow area for several hours.

blocks.caption: Dujuan is Japan's 25th typhoon of the yearImage: Ichiro Ohara/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How have Japan's regions been affected by the incoming storm?
Over 4,000 households in Chiba were without power.
In the central prefecture of Aichi, which is currently hosting the Asian Games, an equestrian eventing competition was postponed until Tuesday.
The Tokyo Game Show, one of the world's biggest video game trade fairs, was shut down ahead of its final day on Monday.
Dujuan could also scupper travel plans during Japan's "Silver Week" holiday, which has just begun and which normally sees a surge in domestic travel.
On Monday, Japan Airlines canceled 120 domestic and 15 international flights, while All Nippon Airways canceled 140 domestic flights.
Some railway services were suspended on some lines in Tokyo and its neighboring areas.
Japan's extreme heat fuels fashion, gadgets to keep cool

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband explains why he forgave her over children's killings
articles.summary: The husband of the US mother who strangled her three young children discusses his grief in an interview with CBS News.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide
Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children, has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her for their deaths.
In an interview with CBS, he also said he did the best he could as his then-wife Lindsay Clancy struggled with mental illness in the months leading up to the day she strangled their children.
Lindsay has not disputed that she killed them but her lawyers argued she should not be held legally responsible because she was suffering from severe mental illness.
A judge declared a mistrial in the case earlier this month after the jury said it could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty of murder.
The prosecution had alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.
Clancy, now 36, was then left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window. She attended the trial in a wheelchair.
Patrick Clancy testified during the trial about his ex-wife's declining mental health after giving birth.
Clancy's team said she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition in which postpartum women can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both.
"I didn't know how to manage a postpartum illness. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive," he told CBS, the BBC's US news partner.
It was her mental health that led to Patrick Clancy deciding later to forgive her.
"I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom', and 'Baby Murderer', 'Monster'. And none of them were accurate," he said in the interview.

"I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever."

Asked if he felt he had failed in some way in this period leading up to the killings, he said: "I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day."
Living with his grief in the weeks after the tragedy became a struggle and he admitted having suicidal thoughts.
"I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it," he said.
During the seven week trial, Patrick was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.
There were claims he was to blame for the murders in some way. Thrust into the limelight, tabloids snapped photos of him travelling and with his new wife Rachel Danis.
The 36-year-old said the speculation was "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children. It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health".
It was also "painful to see" for him personally.
"And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he said.
The intense scrutiny prompted him to move from Duxbury to New York City in a bid to seek anonymity.
Now he is starting a family with Danis and looking forward to telling his future children about their siblings.
"I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids. And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister."
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.
A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

articles.title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
articles.summary: Top US and Chinese officials held talks in New York on Sunday ahead of a Trump-Xi summit this week.

blocks.text: Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday.
Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York.
The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week.

AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks.
He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade.
A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November.
The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment.
Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI.
Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people."
The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries.
In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity.
Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China.
He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins."
In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed.
Those talks ended with an agreement that China would buy Boeing jets and US agricultural goods in exchange for lower tariffs.

articles.title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals
articles.summary: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy…

blocks.text: Nika’s story

blocks.caption: Silhouette of an Iranian woman, DHS officers wrestle a detainee to the ground

blocks.text: No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.
Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.

Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.

Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.

After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.
“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.”

The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?

Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

In order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.

It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.

The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.

A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.

A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.
The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.

Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.
The rug pull

blocks.caption: Trump’s deportation drive is being led by Stephen Miller (left)

blocks.text: Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.

Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.
Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.
Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.

This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.

Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.

For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.

Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”
African deals

blocks.caption: Montage of images, including one of Rabbiatu Kuyateh, government papers and maps

blocks.text: When Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.

A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going”.

blocks.caption: Rabbiatu Kuyateh being forcibly removed from her temporary accommodation in Ghana

blocks.text: Kuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.

She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.
In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.

“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”

The drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire to end most migration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.

Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its name incorporating a term adopted by the far right to describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.

Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 38 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.

They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.

The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.

Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.

On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.
“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.

During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”
Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.

The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”

He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.

One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”
Malaria

blocks.caption: Montage of images including one of a man in handcuffs and one of a persons hand in a hospital bed

blocks.text: Onboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.

blocks.caption: Deportation plane arriving in Bangui on 11 June

blocks.text: For several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.
Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.

US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.

When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”

Back in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.
The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.
The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”

blocks.caption: Montage of images including a cityscape and a woman silhouetted against a window

blocks.text: As the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.
Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.

In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.

According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.

Nika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”

The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.

An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”
Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.

“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”
Life in the shadows

blocks.caption: Montage of images, including of a woman and a man and official US documents

blocks.text: People who had been returned from third countries to the places they were born describe a life now lived in the shadows. Kuyateh left Sierra Leone within days of being sent back there. The Guardian is not naming her location. “I don’t sleep at night,” she said. “Sometimes I just wake up. I’ll be sitting down like, what am I doing here? Why am I here?”

She called her family every day. Sometimes, she said, she felt too sad to turn on the video and see their faces. She could get through the conversation with her mother without tears, she said, “but whenever I talk to my daddy, I’ll be crying. And when I sit here, I think about them. It hurts so much.”
She was not sure what scared her more: the thought of dying alone in a foreign country, or knowing that her parents might die without her at their bedside.

Annan, a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family, said he was terrified when he touched back down in Accra. He had refused to disembark during his initial deportation from the US to Sierra Leone, and had to be forcibly removed from the plane, he said. He later begged authorities not to return him, he said, but they did not listen.

In a statement, the Sierra Leonean government said it took its “international obligations seriously” but that questions relating to immigration protections afforded by an American court were for the US government to address.

It added: “So far, no individual returned to Sierra Leone under the TCNA [third-country national arrangement] has requested to remain in Sierra Leone or not to be returned to his or her country of choice either in west Africa or beyond.”
Annan’s mother had used her savings to pay for his escape to the US. She was distraught when he called to say he was back. “She knew she couldn’t protect me,” he said.

He shared footage of where he lived now: an abandoned building with no electricity or running water in a neighbouring country, he said. He spent his daylight hours hiding, and walked almost an hour to find food when darkness fell. His bed was a blanket on the floor, although he barely slept, he said, too scared of being infected by one of the insects that crawled or buzzed around him. He said the loneliness felt crippling.

In recent weeks, someone had texted him anonymously, saying that his survival, as a gay man, would not be tolerated. The message made him feel hopeless: he could run, it said, but he could not hide for ever.
Exhaustion

blocks.caption: Montage of images including men walking towards a plane and people sitting in a large room

blocks.text: In Los Angeles, Jalili is getting more calls about clients bound for deportation flights. In June, a 30-year-old Iranian woman with a blood disorder that made her so weak she needed a walker was told she would be sent to the landlocked south African nation of Eswatini.
Another client was “going crazy”, Jalili said. “They’re coming up with a new country for her every week.”

Immigration lawyers said that while their jobs had always been hard, the scale of the efforts to obstruct those opposing the Trump administration’s drive to quash all types of irregular migration was unprecedented.

When a client is detained, avenues of accountability have largely been shut, including the office of an independent ombudsman for immigration detention, which was responsible for investigating abuses and misconduct.

In court, immigration lawyers can face hostile judges after the Trump administration purged some of those deemed insufficiently loyal to the deportation agenda. Meanwhile, the cost of even filing a case has risen steeply, under the terms of a bill passed through Congress in July last year.

Jalili, like many others, spent much of the first Trump administration mounting legal challenges against a policy of separating children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Knowing that what would follow might be worse, she decided on the eve of Trump’s re-election to start her own firm to fight the coming storm
It was not uncommon for calls from the desperate families of new ICE detainees to wake her in the night.
One of the biggest challenges, said Erica Reilly, an immigration attorney based in Washington DC, was basic communication with ICE officers.

“You send all these emails to deportation officers, and you’re like: ‘Hi, just following up again on the email I sent you last week, and the week before that, and the week before that, and the week before that, that you haven’t responded to,’” she said. “And they know they don’t have to because there’s no accountability.”
The worst thing, she said, was the powerlessness. But the cruelty and the lack of access, she had come to believe, “that’s all the point”.
“I think that the administration is doing what they can to get enough people to say, well, the alternative is too scary or too uncertain or too bad. I’ll just leave on my own.”
Getting through the day meant reformulating the wins, Reilly said. “Getting a call back from a deportation officer shouldn’t be a win, but in this environment it is.”

Jalili said she did her best to focus on the battles she could win. When she heard Nika’s flight had left for Bangui, she sank to the floor, called her mother, and began to cry. “It’s not a situation where you can just say: ‘Oh, I did my best.’”
Nika had lost the life she knew in Iran. The US offered little better. Jalili listed the cost.

“Being detained for 17 months. Being released from the federal judge’s order for 10 days. Being stripped away from her uncle’s hands. Being put in a car and then on a flight in shackles, and for 24 hours, sitting on that flight. She must have felt so lonely.”
Additional reporting by Alice Speri
